question: is asbestos testing required before they tear down my house
answer: Yes. Before any structural debris removal, an asbestos inspection is required by California air quality regulations. Under the state program, this is handled for you. If you're going the private route, you must hire a certified asbestos consultant and notify your local Air Quality Management District before demolition begins.

question: my mom is 84 and uses a wheelchair her house burned can fema help with accessibility stuff
answer: Yes. FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) can cover disaster-related accessibility needs — like ramps, grab bars, or other modifications — even if those features weren't in the home before, if they're now needed because of the disaster. When applying, make sure to list her functional needs and disability so FEMA flags the case for additional support. Call the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362 and ask about Serious Needs Assistance and accessibility-related repairs. You can also request a home inspector who can accommodate her needs.
topic: Seniors and people with disabilities — special assistance

question: can sba loan be used for upgrades or just repairs
answer: SBA disaster loans generally can't be used to upgrade or add to your home — only to restore it to pre-disaster condition (unless local code requires the upgrade). However, you can request up to a 20% increase above verified damage to pay for mitigation improvements that reduce risk of future disaster damage, like fire-resistant roofing or defensible space.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: can i get my utility bill reduced or paused after a disaster
answer: Yes. California utilities offer emergency disaster relief that can include bill payment extensions, waived deposits, reconnection fee waivers, and rebuilding support. Call your utility directly to request disaster relief, and check the CPUC Consumer Support page (cpuc.ca.gov/consumer-support). Low-income customers may also qualify for CARE or FERA discount programs.

question: Does a federal disaster have to be declared before I can apply?
answer: For FEMA Individual Assistance and SBA disaster loans, yes — a federal or SBA disaster declaration for your county is required. Check current declarations at fema.gov/disasters or sba.gov/disaster. Even without a declaration, you may qualify for state aid, insurance, or nonprofit help — dial 211 to find local resources.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: I'm a renter in a flooded apartment in San Jose and my landlord has insurance on the building — does that cover my stuff?
answer: No. Your landlord's flood policy only covers the building, not your personal belongings. Renters need their own NFIP contents-only policy to be covered for flood damage to furniture, electronics, and clothing. Since you don't have one for this event, apply to FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 — they may help with uninsured personal property losses if your area is in a declared disaster.

question: will my kid still graduate if they missed weeks of school because of the fires
answer: California law protects displaced students — districts must waive coursework students couldn't complete due to the disaster and accept partial credit. Seniors on track to graduate at their original school must be allowed to graduate even if they transfer. Talk to your child's school counselor or the district's homeless liaison to make a plan.

question: hi um i've been having really bad nightmares ever since we evacuated and i can't sleep and i keep thinking the fire is coming back is something wrong with me
answer: Nothing is wrong with you — nightmares, hypervigilance, and trouble sleeping are very common after a disaster and often improve with time and support. Call or text the Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 (24/7, free, multilingual) to talk with a trained counselor. FEMA also funds a Crisis Counseling Program in declared disaster areas — ask your local county behavioral health office, or dial 211 to be connected to free local services.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: i missed the fema inspector when they came by what happens now
answer: Call FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 as soon as possible to reschedule. If you miss the inspection and don't reschedule, your application may be denied. Inspectors usually call to set up a time — make sure FEMA has your current phone number in your DisasterAssistance.gov account.

question: Do I need to remove the dead trees on my property too or is that separate?
answer: Hazard tree removal is often included in the state debris removal program, but only for trees deemed a threat to the right-of-way or public areas — criteria vary by disaster. Trees that pose no public hazard are usually the homeowner's responsibility. Ask your county debris program coordinator for the specific hazard tree assessment process in your area.

question: can i apply for fema and sba at the same time
answer: Yes, and you should. Register with FEMA first at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. FEMA will often refer you to SBA — complete that SBA application at sba.gov/disaster even if you don't want a loan, because it can qualify you for additional FEMA grant money for personal property and transportation.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: what if i already filed a workers comp claim but never heard back
answer: If you filed a DWC-1 and haven't gotten a response, the insurer has 90 days to accept or deny — silence past that means the claim is presumed accepted. Contact the claims administrator directly first, then reach out to the state's Information & Assistance Unit at 1-800-736-7401 for free help. You can also request a free consultation from a workers' comp attorney; most don't charge unless they win.
topic: Workers' comp and job protection during evacuation

question: are fema payments and insurance money taxable income
answer: FEMA disaster assistance grants are generally NOT taxable. Qualified wildfire relief payments under the federal Wildfire Relief Act are also excluded from income for 2020–2025. Insurance payouts for your home/property usually aren't taxable unless they exceed your cost basis (a "gain"), and even then you can often defer it by rebuilding. See the IRS Wildfire Relief Payments FAQ at irs.gov for specifics.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: I rent my apartment, does FEMA help renters too or only homeowners?
answer: Yes, renters are eligible. FEMA can help with temporary housing, replacement of essential personal property (furniture, clothing, appliances), medical/dental, transportation, and other disaster-related expenses. Apply the same way at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362, and have your lease or proof of occupancy ready.

question: can undocumented workers get dua
answer: DUA generally requires you to be authorized to work in the U.S., so undocumented workers usually don't qualify. However, you may still get help from other sources — local nonprofits, mutual aid funds, the Red Cross (1-800-733-2767), and some California state programs don't require immigration status. Call 211 to find local assistance available regardless of status.

question: i lost my drivers license and passport in the fire how do i replace them
answer: For your California driver's license, contact the DMV at 1-800-777-0133 — after declared disasters they often waive replacement fees. For a passport, contact the State Department at travel.state.gov or 1-877-487-2778. Social Security cards can be replaced free at ssa.gov or 1-800-772-1213, and a Disaster Recovery Center can often help you get multiple replacement documents in one visit.

question: my landlord says the apartment is red tagged what does that mean
answer: A red tag means the building was inspected and deemed unsafe to enter or occupy due to earthquake damage. You cannot live there until repairs are made and it's re-inspected. As a renter, you may be eligible for FEMA rental assistance if a federal disaster is declared (apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362). Call 211 for emergency shelter, and contact a legal aid office about getting your security deposit and prorated rent back — try LawHelpCA.org.

question: do i have to file with my insurance before fema
answer: Yes, you should file with your insurance first because FEMA cannot duplicate benefits insurance covers. But don't wait for the insurance decision to register with FEMA — apply right away at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362, and send FEMA your insurance settlement or denial letter when you get it.

question: My mom is 78 and not great with computers, can someone help her apply for FEMA in person?
answer: Absolutely. She can visit a local Disaster Recovery Center (DRC) where FEMA staff will help her apply in person — find the nearest one at fema.gov/drc or by calling 1-800-621-3362. She can also call that number to apply by phone (TTY 1-800-462-7585). You can also apply on her behalf if she gives written authorization.

question: im undocumented can i still get food help after the disaster
answer: Yes. Food banks and most disaster food distributions do not ask about immigration status — anyone can receive free food. While regular CalFresh has citizenship requirements for adults, your U.S. citizen or eligible-immigrant children can still get CalFresh without affecting your status. The California Food Assistance Program (CFAP) also covers some immigrants not eligible for federal SNAP. Using food banks or disaster food aid is not considered a public charge issue.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: what if i dont agree with the denial
answer: You have the right to appeal. Request the denial in writing with the specific policy language cited, then submit a written appeal with supporting documents (estimates, photos, expert opinions). If the insurer still won't budge, file a Request for Assistance with the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357 or insurance.ca.gov — they investigate disputes for free. You can also consult a disaster insurance attorney; many work on contingency for large claims.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: My husband and I own a small farm stand in Sonoma and we lost everything plus our home. Can we apply for both a home loan and a business loan from SBA?
answer: Yes — you can apply for both. File a Home and Personal Property Loan (up to $500K for the home, $100K for belongings) AND a Business Physical Disaster Loan plus EIDL for the farm stand (up to $2 million combined). They're separate applications but you can submit them together at sba.gov/disaster. A Disaster Recovery Center can help you file both in one visit.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: What kind of documentation should I gather before applying for disaster assistance?
answer: Take photos and videos of all damage before cleaning up, and make a written list of damaged or destroyed items. Gather your ID, Social Security number, proof of address (utility bill, lease), proof of homeownership (deed, tax records, mortgage statement), insurance policy info, and bank account info for direct deposit. If documents were destroyed, FEMA and the DMV can help you replace them.

question: how do i get calfresh after the fire
answer: You can apply for CalFresh online at GetCalFresh.org or BenefitsCal.com, by calling your county social services office, or by dialing 2-1-1. After a federally declared disaster, you may also qualify for Disaster CalFresh (D-CalFresh), which has expanded eligibility and faster processing. Benefits are loaded onto an EBT card you can use at most grocery stores and farmers markets.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: hi so my grandfather is 79 he doesnt use computers and his hearing is bad how is he supposed to apply for any of this fema stuff
answer: He has options that don't require a computer. He can call the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362 — they have TTY and can connect through video relay or captioned telephone services if he gives them his relay number. Even better, you or another trusted person can apply on his behalf if he authorizes it, or you can take him to a Disaster Recovery Center where staff will walk him through it in person and provide assistive listening devices. To find the nearest center, text DRC and his ZIP code to 43362.
topic: Seniors and people with disabilities — special assistance

question: I'm a housekeeper and my employer's house burned down, do I qualify for workers comp or unemployment? I got hurt helping them pack before we evacuated
answer: You may have two options. If you were injured on the job (even during evacuation prep), you can file a workers' compensation claim — domestic workers are covered in many situations. Report the injury to your employer in writing and file a DWC-1 form. For lost wages because the home/job is gone, apply for Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) through EDD at edd.ca.gov once a federal disaster is declared. Call 211 if you need help navigating both.
topic: Workers' comp and job protection during evacuation

question: I run a small bakery in Sonoma and we've had no internet for a week so we can't process card payments — is there any disaster help for that?
answer: Yes — small businesses affected by communications outages and other disaster impacts can apply for low-interest SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL), which cover lost revenue and operating expenses. Apply at sba.gov/disaster or call 1-800-659-2955. Also contact your internet provider about disaster credits, and file a complaint with the CPUC (cpuc.ca.gov/consumer-support) if service restoration is delayed. Your local Small Business Development Center (americassbdc.org) can also help you navigate recovery options.

question: i applyed for fema housing help 2 weeks ago and havnt heard anything
answer: Log in to your account at DisasterAssistance.gov or call FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 to check your status — they can tell you if they need more documents, an inspection, or an insurance decision letter. Missing paperwork is the most common cause of delay. If you've been denied or need urgent shelter in the meantime, call 211 for local emergency housing.

question: Hi, my house burned down in the fire and a guy just showed up at my property saying he can start debris removal tomorrow for cash. Should I hire him?
answer: Please be very cautious — this is a classic post-disaster scam pattern. Door-to-door solicitors demanding cash and offering to start immediately are often unlicensed. Before hiring anyone, verify their license at cslb.ca.gov, get a written contract, and never pay more than 10% or $1,000 down (whichever is less). You can also report suspicious contractors to CSLB's Disaster Help Center.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: do i have to look for work while getting dua
answer: Yes, generally you must be able and available to work and accept suitable work if offered, just like regular UI. However, if the disaster makes work search unreasonable (your area is destroyed, you're displaced, etc.), EDD may waive or adjust that requirement. Report honestly on your biweekly certifications and explain your situation.

question: My mom is 78 and doesn't use computers. She lost her ID and birth certificate in the evacuation. How can she replace them without going online?
answer: She has options that don't require a computer. For her driver's license/ID, she can walk into any DMV office — call 1-800-777-0133 to get the nearest location and ask about disaster fee waivers. For her birth certificate, she can visit or mail a request to the county recorder where she was born, or call CA Vital Records at 916-445-2684. A local Disaster Recovery Center (find one at 1-800-621-3362) can also help her in person with FEMA and document replacement referrals.

question: do i have to make a list of everything i lost
answer: Yes, your insurer will ask for a personal property inventory, but you don't have to do it from memory alone. Walk through your home room by room (or use photos/videos you have), check old receipts, Amazon and credit card history, and social media photos to reconstruct what you owned. Include brand, age, and estimated replacement cost. Take your time — insurers must give you a reasonable period, and California extends this for declared disasters.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: hi so our house burned in the eaton fire and honestly i have no idea where to even start with insurance, can you walk me through it?
answer: So sorry you're going through this. First, call your homeowners insurance company's claims line (it's on your policy or their website) to open a claim and get a claim number. Ask specifically about Additional Living Expenses (ALE) — that covers hotels, rentals, food, and pet boarding while you're displaced, and many insurers will advance you funds right away. Then document everything you can remember owning (photos, receipts, even credit card statements help) and save every receipt going forward. If you hit problems, the California Department of Insurance can help at 1-800-927-4357.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: What is Disaster CalFresh and how is it different from regular CalFresh?
answer: Disaster CalFresh (D-CalFresh or D-SNAP) is a temporary food benefit program activated after a federally declared disaster. It has higher income limits than regular CalFresh and counts disaster expenses like home repairs, evacuation costs, and lost income. Benefits are usually one month of food assistance on an EBT card. It's only available during a specific application window announced by CDSS, so check cdss.ca.gov or call 2-1-1 for current openings.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: How long do I have to wait before my first SBA disaster loan payment is due?
answer: SBA disaster loans defer your first payment for 12 months from the date of the note, and interest does not accrue during that deferment period. This gives you time to focus on recovery before repayment begins. You can manage your loan and check status through the MySBA Loan Portal.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: lost policy in fire how do i find insurance info
answer: Call your insurance agent or the company directly — they can look you up by name and address. If you don't remember the company, check your mortgage lender (they're listed as a payee), bank statements for premium payments, or your email for renewal notices. The California Department of Insurance can also help locate your policy at 1-800-927-4357.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: where do i register for fema
answer: You can register for FEMA assistance online at DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-3362, or by visiting a Disaster Recovery Center in person. Have your Social Security number, insurance info, and damage description ready when you apply.

question: what if i already filed but never heard back
answer: Log into your account at DisasterAssistance.gov to check your status, or call the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362. Make sure FEMA has your current phone number and address — missed inspection calls are a common reason for delays. Decisions are usually issued within about 10 days after your home inspection.

question: i'm 72 and live alone, my basement flooded and i can't do the cleanup myself, is there anyone who can help with the mold?
answer: You don't have to do this alone. Call 211 to be connected with local disaster case management and volunteer cleanup groups — organizations like Crisis Cleanup (1-844-965-1386), Team Rubicon, and Samaritan's Purse often provide free muck-out and mold cleanup for older adults and people with disabilities after disasters. Also apply for FEMA assistance at 1-800-621-3362 — Clean and Sanitize funds may help cover professional remediation.

question: How do I get a replacement birth certificate in California after a wildfire?
answer: You can request a certified copy of a California birth certificate from the CA Department of Public Health Vital Records (cdph.ca.gov) or from the county recorder's office where you were born — the county is usually faster. Fees may be waived if you're a disaster survivor in a declared area; ask the county recorder. You'll need to fill out a sworn statement and provide some form of ID, but counties can often work with you if your ID was also destroyed.

question: What is the deadline to apply for FEMA assistance after a disaster?
answer: The standard deadline to register for FEMA Individual Assistance is 60 days after the disaster is declared, though FEMA sometimes extends it. Check the exact deadline for your disaster at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362. Don't wait — apply as soon as possible even if you're still gathering documents.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: what should be in a contract with a contractor for rebuilding
answer: A California home improvement contract must be in writing and include: the contractor's name, address, and license number; a detailed scope of work and materials; total price and payment schedule; start and completion dates; a 3-day right to cancel; and down payment no more than 10% or $1,000 (whichever is less). Never sign a blank contract or pay in full upfront. CSLB's 'Terms of Agreement' consumer guide at cslb.ca.gov has a full checklist.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: Can I get FEMA help if I already have flood insurance?
answer: Yes, but FEMA assistance is secondary to insurance — they won't duplicate benefits. File your NFIP claim first, then apply to FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. FEMA may help with needs your flood policy doesn't cover (like additional living expenses if you lack ALE coverage) or provide gap assistance if your settlement is delayed. Send FEMA your insurance settlement documents once you have them.

question: is the disater distres hotline really free
answer: Yes — the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline (1-800-985-5990) is 100% free, confidential, and available 24/7/365. You can call or text, and interpreters are available in over 100 languages. They won't ask for your name, insurance, or immigration status.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: Does FEMA cover veterinary bills if my pet was injured in the wildfire?
answer: FEMA's Individuals and Households Program generally does not cover veterinary expenses for pets. However, organizations like RedRover Relief, the ASPCA, and the California Veterinary Medical Association's Disaster Relief Fund offer grants for emergency vet care after disasters. Your local Humane Society or Animal Services may also provide free or low-cost treatment for disaster-affected pets — call 2-1-1 for referrals.

question: do i need to apply for the irs extension
answer: No — the IRS applies disaster relief automatically based on the address on your most recent tax return. If you moved into the disaster area after filing, or your records were located there, call 1-866-562-5227 to request relief manually.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: my 6 year old wont stop crying about the fire what do i do
answer: It's very common for young kids to have strong reactions after a disaster. Keep routines as normal as possible, give extra hugs and reassurance, limit news/social media exposure, and let them talk or draw about their feelings. For free 24/7 support, call the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 (they help parents too, and have counselors who can guide you). If symptoms last more than a few weeks, contact your pediatrician.
topic: Emotional support for children after a disaster

question: Hi, my house flooded about 2 weeks ago during the storms and now I'm seeing black spots on the walls and it smells musty, I have two little kids and I'm worried about their health, what should I do?
answer: Your concern is valid — mold can trigger asthma and allergies, especially in children. Keep your kids out of affected rooms until cleanup is done. For areas larger than about 10 square feet, hire a professional mold remediation contractor. Smaller areas can be cleaned with detergent and water (don't mix bleach with ammonia). FEMA's 'Clean and Sanitize' assistance under Other Needs Assistance may cover some costs — apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. Call 211 for local health resources.

question: what about school meals if school is closed
answer: Many districts continue free meal distribution at alternate sites during closures — check your district's website or call them directly. You can also call 211 to find emergency food resources and meal sites near you. If the disaster qualifies, families may also receive D-SNAP (Disaster CalFresh) benefits to replace school meals.

question: How does SBA decide how much I can borrow for my business?
answer: SBA reviews verified physical damage (buildings, equipment, inventory) and your ability to repay based on credit and cash flow. Businesses can borrow up to $2 million combined for physical damage and economic injury. Insurance proceeds are deducted from the eligible amount, and you may get up to a 20% increase for mitigation improvements.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: where can i bord my horses durring the evacuaton
answer: Many California counties open large-animal evacuation sites at fairgrounds during wildfires and floods — for example, Pierce College, Industry Hills, and county fairgrounds are commonly used in Southern CA. Call your county Animal Services or 2-1-1 for the current large-animal shelter location. Groups like the Humane Society Equine Rescue and local CART (County Animal Response Team) volunteers can also help with transport if you can't move the horses yourself.

question: my boss is making us come in even though theres a evacuation warning is that leagal
answer: You have the right to refuse work you reasonably believe is unsafe under California Labor Code 6311, and Cal/OSHA's wildfire smoke standard (section 5141.1) requires employers to protect workers when AQI exceeds 151. Your employer cannot retaliate against you for refusing unsafe work or for evacuating under a mandatory order. Report violations to Cal/OSHA at 1-833-579-0927 or file a retaliation complaint with the Labor Commissioner.
topic: Workers' comp and job protection during evacuation

question: how do i no if my house is safe to go back in after earthqauke
answer: Wait for local officials or your city's building department to inspect and clear the area. Look for warning signs: cracks in the foundation, leaning walls, a damaged chimney, broken gas lines, or doors/windows that won't close. If you smell gas, hear hissing, or see downed power lines, leave immediately and call 911 or your utility. Many California cities run free post-quake safety assessment programs — call 211 to find one near you.

question: do nonprofits qualify for sba disaster loans
answer: Yes, most private nonprofit organizations located in a declared disaster area are eligible for SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) and Physical Disaster Loans. The same terms apply — up to $2 million combined, payments deferred 12 months, and interest capped at 4% (lower for nonprofits in many cases). Apply at sba.gov/disaster or call 800-659-2955.

question: what if i already filed but never heard back
answer: Call FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 with your registration number ready, or log in at DisasterAssistance.gov to see your status and any pending document requests. Often the application is waiting on your insurance settlement letter or an inspection. If you're still without housing, call 211 for emergency shelter help while you wait.

question: I already filed a Notice of Loss with FSA weeks ago for my flooded strawberry fields but haven't heard anything back, what should I do?
answer: Call your local FSA county office directly and ask for a status update on your Notice of Loss and which program application (NAP, ELAP, or Emergency Loan) it's tied to. Processing can be slow after major disasters, so ask if they need any additional documentation like production records, receipts, or photos. If you can't get a response, you can contact the California FSA state office or your USDA Service Center supervisor. Keep written notes of every call and the names of staff you speak with.

question: gas smell after earthquake
answer: Leave the building immediately — don't use light switches, phones, or anything that could spark. Once outside and safely away, call 911 and your gas utility (PG&E: 1-800-743-5000; SoCalGas: 1-800-427-2200). If you know how, shut off gas at the meter using a wrench (quarter turn). Do not turn it back on yourself — only the utility can safely restore service.

question: can i get fired for evacuating from the fire
answer: California law generally protects workers who evacuate due to a declared emergency. Labor Code 1102 and 6311 prohibit retaliation against employees who refuse to work in unsafe conditions, and Governor's emergency proclamations often include job protections. If you were fired for evacuating, file a retaliation complaint with the CA Labor Commissioner at 833-526-4636 or file with Cal/OSHA if it was a safety issue.
topic: Workers' comp and job protection during evacuation

question: does fema pay for medicial bills from the disater
answer: Yes, FEMA's Individuals and Households Program can provide money for disaster-caused medical and dental expenses not covered by insurance — things like injuries from the event, replacement of medical equipment, or prescription costs. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362, and keep all receipts and bills. Medicaid/Medi-Cal and your health insurance should be billed first.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: Hi, our house got flooded last week and we're back home now but I'm scared to let my kids drink from the tap, how do I know if the water is okay?
answer: If you're on a public water system, check with your utility — they'll issue a boil-water notice if the supply is unsafe, and lift it once tests pass. You can usually find updates on their website or by calling them directly. If you're on a private well, don't drink it until it's been disinfected (shock chlorinated) and tested for coliform bacteria and E. coli by a state-certified lab. Until then, use bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, and making baby formula.

question: What documents do I need to apply for DUA?
answer: You'll generally need your Social Security number, a government-issued ID, proof of employment or self-employment at the time of the disaster (pay stubs, tax returns, 1099s, or a letter from your employer), and proof that the disaster caused your job loss. You must submit proof of income within 21 days of filing your DUA claim, so gather documents early.

question: where do i drop off clothes for fire victims
answer: Please don't drop donations at disaster sites — unsolicited goods often overwhelm responders. Instead, call 211 (or visit 211ca.org) to find local organizations actively accepting donations. Cash donations to vetted groups like the American Red Cross, CA Community Foundation Wildfire Recovery Fund, or local food banks are usually the most helpful. You can also check CaliforniaVolunteers.ca.gov for current needs.

question: lost my id in the fire how do i replace it
answer: You can apply for a replacement California ID card through the DMV. Start the application online at dmv.ca.gov, but you'll need to visit a DMV office to finish (photo and thumbprint). The replacement fee may be waived for disaster survivors in declared areas — ask the DMV about a fee waiver when you go in. Make a DMV appointment online to skip the long wait.

question: Can FEMA replace my dad's CPAP machine and wheelchair that were destroyed in the fire?
answer: Yes. FEMA's Personal Property Assistance under IHP can help replace disaster-damaged medical equipment like CPAP machines, wheelchairs, walkers, hearing aids, and prescription eyeglasses — and you do NOT need a doctor's note for items he owned before the disaster. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362, and list each item with an estimated replacement cost. If insurance or Medicare won't cover the replacement, FEMA may.
topic: Seniors and people with disabilities — special assistance

question: How much does the state debris removal program cost homeowners?
answer: The CalRecycle-led debris removal program has no out-of-pocket cost to property owners. However, if your insurance policy specifically covers debris removal, you may be required to remit those proceeds to the program. You won't pay more than what your insurance covers — uninsured costs are absorbed by state and federal funding.

question: hi so we evacuated last night with our two cats and a parrot and the shelter they sent us to said no pets allowed, what do we do? we have nowhere else to go
answer: I'm sorry — that's stressful. Please call 2-1-1 right away; they can locate the nearest pet-friendly shelter or co-located animal shelter for your cats and bird. You can also contact your county Animal Services or the local Humane Society, which often set up emergency boarding during disasters. The SPCA and organizations like RedRover sometimes provide free emergency sheltering and transport for evacuees' pets — ask 2-1-1 to connect you.

question: is there any cash help for undocumentd familys in california after a disater
answer: Yes. California has previously activated the Disaster Relief Assistance for Immigrants (DRAI) program, which provides direct cash aid to undocumented adults who don't qualify for federal help. Availability depends on the disaster declaration — check with your county's social services or call 211. Local nonprofits like CHIRLA, Catholic Charities, and CARECEN also offer emergency cash, food, and rental assistance regardless of status.

question: what if i already hired a private contractor to remove my debris
answer: You can still opt out of the government program and use a private contractor — this is called the Private Property Debris Removal (PPDR) or alternative program. You'll need to submit a work plan to your county/local environmental health department for approval before work begins, and the contractor must be licensed and follow the same safety and disposal standards. Keep all receipts; some costs may be reimbursable through insurance or FEMA.

question: do i need to file with insurance before fema
answer: Yes — file your insurance claim first. FEMA cannot duplicate benefits your insurance covers, but it may help with uninsured or underinsured losses. Still apply with FEMA right away (1-800-621-3362 or DisasterAssistance.gov) even while your insurance claim is pending; you can submit your insurance settlement letter to FEMA later.

question: Hi, my home in Altadena burned down in the Eaton Fire and I want to rebuild the same house I had before, do I have to follow new zoning rules or can I just rebuild what was there?
answer: In most California disaster zones, you can rebuild 'like-for-like' (same footprint, height, and use) without a full new zoning review, even if current codes would normally require something different. However, you'll still need to meet current building, fire, and wildland-urban interface (WUI) codes (Chapter 7A) for safety. LA County's Unincorporated Disaster Recovery Permitting program waives many fees and expedites review for like-for-like rebuilds. Contact LA County Public Works' Rebuild LA Recovery Center or visit recovery.lacounty.gov for specifics.
topic: Long-term recovery: rebuilding permits and zoning

question: Hi, I lost almost everything in the wildfire and I'm completely overwhelmed. Where do I even start to get help?
answer: I'm so sorry for your loss. Start by registering with FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362 — this opens the door to grants for temporary housing, repairs, and other needs. Then file a claim with your insurance company (FEMA needs that info too). Finally, you can apply for a low-interest SBA disaster loan at sba.gov/disaster, which is available to homeowners, renters, and businesses. Also dial 211 for local recovery resources.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: My elderly mother lost her home and she doesn't really use computers, how can she file an insurance claim?
answer: She can file by phone — every insurance company has a 24/7 claims phone line, usually printed on billing statements or available by calling the main customer service number. An adjuster will be assigned and can meet her in person. If she'd like help advocating, the California Department of Insurance offers free assistance at 1-800-927-4357, and Disaster Recovery Centers have insurance specialists who can sit down with her face-to-face.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: How much money will I get from DUA?
answer: Your DUA weekly benefit is calculated similarly to regular UI based on your recent earnings, with a minimum set by federal rules and a maximum that matches California's UI max (currently $450/week). Self-employed applicants' benefits are based on net income from tax returns. Benefits can last up to 26 weeks from the start of the disaster.

question: I filed for the disaster extension months ago and still haven't heard back, is that normal?
answer: You shouldn't expect a confirmation letter — disaster relief is applied automatically to your account based on your address, so there's nothing to "approve." If you received a late-filing or late-payment notice anyway, call the number on the notice or the IRS disaster hotline at 1-866-562-5227 and mention the disaster; they'll abate the penalty. You can also check your account status at irs.gov/account.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: how do i uplaod docs to fema if my internt keeps cutting out
answer: A few tips: (1) Try uploading from a public Wi-Fi spot like a library, Disaster Recovery Center, or community center — 211 can help locate one. (2) If uploads keep failing, you can mail documents to FEMA or bring them in person to a Disaster Recovery Center. (3) You can also fax documents to 1-800-827-8112. (4) If you need help with your online account, call 1-844-875-6446. Documents may take up to 10 days to show in your Upload History.

question: i already paid a contractor 20k upfront and now hes not returning calls what do i do
answer: File a complaint with CSLB immediately at cslb.ca.gov (select 'Licensed and Unlicensed Project Complaints') or call 1-800-321-2752. Document everything — contract, payments, texts, photos. If he was unlicensed and took more than $1,000 or didn't deliver, that may be a crime; also file a report with your local police or DA's consumer fraud unit. If he was licensed, you may be able to recover funds through his contractor bond.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: My elderly mother lives alone and can't drive to a food pantry. Are there delivery options?
answer: Yes — many California food banks offer home delivery for seniors and people with disabilities. Call 2-1-1 to find programs in her area, or contact her local Area Agency on Aging (eldercare.acl.gov or 1-800-510-2020). Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to homebound seniors. If she has CalFresh, she can also use it to order groceries online from Amazon, Walmart, Safeway, and Albertsons with delivery.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: hi so my house burned down in the fire and theres ash everywhere can i just start cleaning it up myself or is that dangerous?
answer: Please do not touch or breathe in the ash — wildfire debris often contains toxic materials like asbestos, lead, and heavy metals. Wait for the official Phase 1 hazardous household waste removal (handled by US EPA or state crews) before any cleanup begins. After that, you can either opt into the state-sponsored Phase 2 debris removal program through your county at no out-of-pocket cost, or hire a licensed private contractor. Contact your county recovery office to sign up.

question: fema denied me what now
answer: Don't panic — many denials are due to missing documents and can be fixed on appeal. You have 60 days from the date of your decision letter to appeal. Submit any missing paperwork (insurance settlement, proof of occupancy/ownership, repair estimates) through your DisasterAssistance.gov account, by mail, or by fax to (800) 827-8112. Call 1-800-621-3362 if you need help understanding the letter.

question: can my landlord evict me if my apartment burned down
answer: Generally no — if the unit is uninhabitable due to a disaster, California law (Civil Code 1933) typically ends the lease obligation, but your landlord cannot simply evict you without proper notice. You may be entitled to a prorated refund of rent and your security deposit for the time the unit was unusable. Contact Disaster Legal Services (free) by calling 211 or your local Legal Aid office. You can also call the CA Attorney General's office for tenant rights questions.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: Hi, my husband and I lost both of our cars in the Eaton fire and we only had liability insurance on one of them, is there anything we can do to get help replacing them because we need to get to work?
answer: I'm so sorry. Without comprehensive coverage, insurance won't pay for the fire loss, but you still have options. Apply to FEMA (1-800-621-3362 or DisasterAssistance.gov) — they offer limited Transportation Assistance if a vehicle is essential and uninsured. Then apply for an SBA disaster home loan, which can lend up to $100,000 for personal property including vehicle replacement, at low interest rates. You may also qualify for a casualty loss deduction on your taxes — see IRS disaster relief guidance.
topic: Replacing a car or vehicle damaged in disaster

question: Hi, our house burned down last week and we lost everything including our birth certificates, social security cards, and drivers licenses. Where do we even start?
answer: I'm so sorry. Start with the documents you'll need first to access aid: (1) Driver's license/ID — apply at dmv.ca.gov, fees are often waived for disaster survivors. (2) Birth certificates — order from the CA Department of Public Health Vital Records or your county recorder. (3) Social Security card — request a replacement free at ssa.gov/myaccount or call 1-800-772-1213. FEMA does NOT require these originals to register — call 1-800-621-3362 or go to DisasterAssistance.gov to apply now and submit documents later.

question: How long do I have to rebuild before insurance stops paying?
answer: Under California law, after a declared disaster you have at least 36 months to rebuild and collect full replacement cost benefits, and you can request additional extensions of 6 months for good cause. You're also allowed to rebuild at a different location or buy an already-built replacement home and still receive your full replacement cost benefits. Keep your insurer updated in writing on your rebuilding progress.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: How does Additional Living Expenses coverage actually work?
answer: ALE (also called Loss of Use) reimburses the extra costs of living away from home — hotel, rental, restaurant meals above normal grocery costs, laundry, pet boarding, and storage. Save every receipt and keep a simple log. In California declared disasters, insurers must offer at least 24 months of ALE (extendable to 36) and must advance at least 4 months of ALE upon request without requiring an itemized inventory.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: how long does it take to get aproved for calfesh
answer: Regular CalFresh applications are processed within 30 days, but if you have very low income and resources you may qualify for expedited service — benefits within 3 days. Disaster CalFresh is even faster, often issued within a few days during the application window. Apply at GetCalFresh.org or BenefitsCal.com.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: my house burned down and i cant get mail how do i get my edd payments
answer: Two options: First, sign up for direct deposit or the EDD debit card through myEDD so you don't rely on mail. Second, if you're already receiving paper mail, contact your local post office about holding or forwarding mail, or call USPS at 1-800-275-8777. You can also call EDD at 1-800-300-5616 to update your address.

question: what if i was denied by sba
answer: If SBA denies your disaster loan, you may automatically become eligible for additional FEMA assistance — so don't ignore the denial letter. You can also appeal the SBA decision within 6 months by submitting new information (updated income, corrected credit issues, etc.). Keep the denial letter; FEMA may ask to see it.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: i filed for dua like 3 weeks ago and havent heard anything what do i do
answer: Log in to myEDD to check your claim status and look for any messages or requests for documents — DUA claims often need extra paperwork like tax returns or proof of employment. If everything looks submitted, call EDD at 1-800-300-5616 to ask about the delay. Disaster claim volume is high, so processing can take several weeks.

question: I run a small dairy farm in the Central Valley and we just got hit by flooding, who tests our water for the cows and the milking equipment?
answer: For agricultural operations, contact your county environmental health department and your local UC Cooperative Extension office — they can advise on testing for livestock water and dairy sanitation. You'll need a state-certified (ELAP) lab to test for coliform, E. coli, and possibly nitrates. The CDFA Dairy Safety Branch may also need to clear your milking system before you resume shipping milk. SBA disaster loans can help cover testing and remediation costs.

question: My elderly mom doesn't use the internet. How can she apply for disaster aid without going online?
answer: She can apply by phone at 1-800-621-3362 (TTY 1-800-462-7585), open 7 a.m.–11 p.m. ET, 7 days a week, with help available in many languages. She can also visit a Disaster Recovery Center in person — find the nearest one at fema.gov/drc or by calling that same number. Staff there will walk her through the application.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: are aftershocks dangerous should i worry
answer: Yes — aftershocks can be strong enough to bring down already-weakened buildings, chimneys, and walls. Stay out of damaged structures, watch for falling debris, and keep shoes on in case of broken glass. If you're indoors during an aftershock, drop, cover, and hold on. Aftershocks can continue for days, weeks, or months after a major quake.

question: I'm an undocumented farmworker and I take care of the owner's horses, can I call for evacuation help without getting in trouble?
answer: Yes — animal rescue and evacuation services do not ask about immigration status. Call 211, county Animal Services, or local CART volunteers; they're focused on saving animals, not enforcement. The Red Cross and county shelters also serve everyone regardless of status. If you need to leave the property yourself, evacuation shelters are open to all residents too.
topic: Livestock and large animal evacuation and recovery

question: disability help fema
answer: FEMA offers extra support for people with disabilities, including accessible communication (ASL, large print, Braille), accessible Disaster Recovery Centers, and funds to replace lost medical equipment or make accessibility repairs. Call the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362 (TTY available, or use your video/captioned relay service) and tell them about your access or functional needs. You can also ask for a Disability Integration Advisor at any Disaster Recovery Center.
topic: Seniors and people with disabilities — special assistance

question: how long can i stay in a fema hotel
answer: FEMA's Transitional Sheltering Assistance (TSA), when activated, typically covers short stays of about 5–14 days at a time and can be extended based on need and the disaster. FEMA reviews eligibility periodically. Call 1-800-621-3362 or check your account at DisasterAssistance.gov for your specific end date and extension options.

question: how do i find my catttle that ran off durring the fire
answer: Report missing livestock to your county Animal Services, the county Agricultural Commissioner, and CDFA's Animal Health Branch — they coordinate stray livestock recovery after disasters. Post photos and brand/ear tag info to local lost livestock Facebook groups and your county CART page. Neighboring ranchers often round up displaced animals, so check with the local cattlemen's association too. Keep brand inspection paperwork handy to prove ownership when claiming them.
topic: Livestock and large animal evacuation and recovery

question: hi so i got a letter from fema saying i was only approved for like $800 but my house has way more damage than that what can i do
answer: You can appeal FEMA's decision within 60 days of the date on your letter. Gather documents that show the full extent of damage — repair estimates from contractors, receipts, photos, and insurance settlement letters if you have them. Write down why the amount isn't enough and include the appeal form (or just a letter) with your FEMA application number and disaster number on every page. Submit it through your DisasterAssistance.gov account, by mail, or by fax to (800) 827-8112.

question: my water isnt working since the fire who do i call
answer: Contact your local water provider — the number is usually on your water bill or your city/county website. After wildfires, water systems sometimes issue Do Not Drink or Boil Water notices due to contamination, so check for those notices before using tap water. If you can't reach your provider, call 211 for local water distribution sites.

question: Are there free counseling services available for disaster survivors in California?
answer: Yes. FEMA's Crisis Counseling Assistance and Training Program (CCP) funds free, confidential, short-term counseling for survivors in federally declared disaster areas, delivered through California county behavioral health departments. You can also call 211 (or visit 211ca.org) to find local mental health resources, or contact the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990, available 24/7 in multiple languages.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: can i bring my dog to the shelter
answer: Many Red Cross and county-run disaster shelters in California are pet-friendly or have co-located pet shelters nearby, but policies vary by location. Call 2-1-1 to find the closest shelter that accepts pets, and bring a leash/carrier, vaccination records, food, and any medications if possible. Service animals are always allowed in all shelters by law.

question: I'm undocumented — can my family stay in a shelter?
answer: Yes. Emergency shelters run by the Red Cross, local governments, and nonprofits in California do not ask about immigration status and are open to everyone. While undocumented adults can't apply for FEMA directly, you may apply on behalf of a U.S. citizen child in your household, and California has state-funded disaster relief programs that don't require status. Call 211 for shelter and resources in your area.

question: se habla espanol en la linea de crisis
answer: Sí. The Disaster Distress Helpline (1-800-985-5990) has Spanish-speaking counselors 24/7 — you can press 2 for Spanish, or text "Hablanos" to 1-800-985-5990. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline also offers Spanish service by pressing 2. Both are free and confidential, regardless of immigration status.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: how do i aply for the livestoc indemnty program after my cattle died in the fire
answer: File a Notice of Loss with your local USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) office within 30 days of when the loss was apparent. For the Livestock Indemnity Program (LIP), you'll need proof the deaths were caused by the disaster — photos, vet records, rendering receipts, or third-party statements work. Then submit form CCC-852 along with documentation of inventory. Visit farmers.gov/recover or call your county FSA office to get started.

question: i own a small bakery and the earthquake damaged my equipment and storefront, what kind of help is out there for businesses
answer: You have a few options. The SBA offers low-interest disaster loans for businesses — up to $2 million for physical damage and economic injury (disasterloanassistance.sba.gov or 1-800-659-2955). Check if your commercial policy includes earthquake coverage and file a claim immediately with photos. Cal OES and your county may open a Local Assistance Center with business recovery resources, and the CA Office of the Small Business Advocate (calosba.ca.gov) can connect you to local relief grants and counseling.

question: hi so my mom is 78 and she takes like 6 different medications and we had to evacuate without them, the pharmacy she uses is in the evacuation zone, what should we do?
answer: I'm sorry you're dealing with this. First, call any pharmacy from the same chain (CVS, Walgreens, Rite Aid, etc.) — they can usually pull her prescription history and do an emergency refill. If she uses an independent pharmacy, call her doctor's office or an urgent care for an emergency supply. California often issues emergency prescription refill orders during declared disasters, so pharmacies can dispense without the original bottle. Dial 211 for local disaster medical help if you get stuck.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: Hi, my church group wants to come down this weekend and help clean up debris from the fires, who do we coordinate with?
answer: Thank you for wanting to help! Please don't self-deploy — affected areas often have safety hazards and access restrictions. Register your group through CaliforniaVolunteers.ca.gov or call 211 to be matched with a vetted Voluntary Organization Active in Disaster (VOAD) partner like Team Rubicon, Samaritan's Purse, or the Mennonite Disaster Service. They'll coordinate timing, training, and safety gear so your group can actually be put to work.

question: green card lost in fire help
answer: You can replace your Permanent Resident Card by filing Form I-90 with USCIS at uscis.gov/i-90. USCIS may waive the filing fee for disaster survivors — submit Form I-912 (fee waiver) with proof you were affected. While you wait, you can request an ADIT stamp (temporary proof of status) by making an InfoPass appointment at 1-800-375-5283. Don't delay — you'll need this for FEMA, work, and benefits.

question: my flood claim got denyed can i apeal
answer: Yes. You have the right to appeal an NFIP claim denial or a payment amount you disagree with. Submit a written appeal to FEMA within 60 days of the denial letter, including supporting documents like photos, receipts, repair estimates, and your adjuster's report. Details and the appeal address are at floodsmart.gov/recover/appeal-a-claim, or call 1-800-621-3362.

question: how do i apply for dua
answer: You can apply for Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) through myEDD at edd.ca.gov, or by calling EDD at 1-800-300-5616 Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. Pacific Time. DUA is only available when the President declares a federal disaster, so check that your area qualifies. Apply as soon as possible — there are deadlines after the disaster declaration.

question: can i rebuild on my lot right away
answer: Not immediately — your property has to be cleared of hazardous materials and debris first (Phase 1 hazardous waste removal, then Phase 2 structural debris removal through CalRecycle or a private contractor approved by your county). After that, you'll need permits from your local building department; many counties set up expedited rebuild permit centers after major fires. Check with your county's Recovery or Building department for current rebuild guidance.

question: how long does FEMA aproval take
answer: After you apply, FEMA usually schedules a home inspection within a few days, and you can typically expect a decision letter within about 10 days of the inspection. You'll get the letter by mail or email depending on your preference. You can check status anytime at DisasterAssistance.gov.

question: What is the deadline to file a homeowners insurance claim after a wildfire in California?
answer: California law requires insurers to give you at least 12 months from the date of loss to file a claim after a declared disaster, and the Insurance Commissioner often extends this further for major events. However, you should notify your insurer as soon as possible — waiting can delay your Additional Living Expenses and repair payments. Check your specific policy's notice requirements, and call the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357 if you need help.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: Hi, we just evacuated and I have three kids and no food in the car, is there somewhere we can get groceries or a hot meal tonight?
answer: I'm sorry you're going through this. Call or text 2-1-1 (or visit 211ca.org) to find the nearest open shelter, food bank, and hot meal site — they're available 24/7 in every California county. Red Cross shelters typically provide free meals, snacks, and water. If you're at an evacuation center, ask staff about emergency food vouchers and Disaster CalFresh enrollment.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: can i start cleaning up before the adjuster comes
answer: Do not throw anything away until the adjuster has documented the damage, but you can take steps to prevent further damage (tarping a roof, boarding windows) — save those receipts, they're reimbursable. Take extensive photos and video of all damage before any cleanup. If the adjuster is delayed, ask your insurer in writing for permission to proceed.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: hi we have a small ranch with about 20 goats and 4 horses and the fire is getting close, we dont have enough trailers to move everyone what do we do
answer: Call your county Animal Services right away and 211 — they can coordinate volunteer trailer help through local CART teams, the Humane Society, and equine rescue networks. If evacuation isn't possible in time, move animals to the largest cleared/irrigated area on your property, remove halters with synthetic parts, write your phone number on their hooves or use livestock crayon on their coats, and leave gates open so they can flee fire. Don't tie or pen them. Notify CDFA and your county ag commissioner once you're safe so they know animals were left behind.
topic: Livestock and large animal evacuation and recovery

question: mold everywhere after flood what do i do
answer: Act fast — mold can grow within 24-48 hours. Remove wet materials (carpet, drywall, insulation), dry the area with fans/dehumidifiers, and clean hard surfaces with detergent and water. Wear an N95 mask, gloves, and goggles. FEMA may provide 'Clean and Sanitize' assistance — apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362. For health questions, call 211.

question: can i apeal fema desicion if i missed the 60 day deadline
answer: Appeals are generally due within 60 days of the date on your FEMA decision letter. If you missed the deadline, you can still try to submit your appeal with a written explanation of why it's late — FEMA may consider it if you had a good reason (illness, displacement, etc.). Call the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362 to discuss your situation before submitting.

question: lost my insulin in the fire what do i do
answer: For immediate medical needs call 911 or go to the nearest ER — they can give you emergency insulin. For replacement prescriptions, contact your pharmacy (chains like CVS/Walgreens can often refill from their system even without the bottle) or call 211 for local disaster medical resources. FEMA's Individuals and Households Program may also reimburse disaster-related medical and prescription costs once you apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: what is a psps
answer: PSPS stands for Public Safety Power Shutoff. Utilities like PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E proactively turn off power during high fire-risk weather (strong winds, dry conditions) to prevent their equipment from sparking wildfires. You can sign up for PSPS alerts at your utility's website using your address — even if you're not the account holder.

question: can i get copies of my old tax returns if they burned up
answer: Yes, and the IRS waives the fee for disaster victims. Request transcripts free at irs.gov/transcripts, or file Form 4506-T (write the disaster name in red at the top, e.g., "California Wildfires") to get free copies. You can also call 1-800-908-9946.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: no cell service since the fire how do i apply to fema
answer: You can still apply to FEMA even without cell service. Try these options: (1) Use any working Wi-Fi (library, shelter, Disaster Recovery Center) to apply at DisasterAssistance.gov, (2) Call FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 from a landline or borrowed phone, or (3) Visit a Disaster Recovery Center in person — staff there can register you and you can use their internet. Find the nearest center at fema.gov/drc.

question: Can I get DUA and FEMA assistance at the same time?
answer: Yes — DUA (income replacement from EDD) and FEMA Individual Assistance (housing, repairs, other needs) are separate programs and you can receive both. You should apply for each one individually: DUA through myEDD or 1-800-300-5616, and FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. You may also qualify for an SBA disaster loan to cover uninsured losses.

question: can i volunteer if im undocumented
answer: Yes — volunteer organizations generally do not ask about immigration status. You can sign up through CaliforniaVolunteers.ca.gov, 211, or directly with groups like World Central Kitchen, local food banks, or mutual aid networks. Some roles (like those requiring a background check or driving an official vehicle) may have more requirements, but most disaster volunteer work does not. Mutual aid groups in your area are often a welcoming starting point.

question: my job burned down in the fire and i cant work now, is there unemployment for that?
answer: Yes — you may qualify for Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) through California's EDD, even if you wouldn't normally qualify for regular unemployment (including self-employed workers and farmworkers). Apply at edd.ca.gov or call 1-800-300-5616, and mention it's a disaster claim. You usually have to apply within 30 days of the DUA announcement for your disaster.

question: i missed the fema deadline what do i do
answer: Call FEMA right away at 1-800-621-3362 and explain why you couldn't apply on time — late applications are sometimes accepted with a valid reason (illness, displacement, etc.). FEMA also occasionally extends deadlines. If you're denied, you can still appeal within 60 days of the decision letter, and free disaster legal aid is available — call 211 for a referral.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: hello i am renter not owner, the fire damaged my apartment building and landlord says we cant come back, does FEMA help renters too or only homeowners
answer: Yes, FEMA helps renters too. You can qualify for Rental Assistance to pay for a new temporary place, Displacement Assistance for immediate lodging, and Personal Property assistance to replace belongings like furniture and clothing. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. Also call 211 for local rental listings and legal aid if you have questions about your lease.

question: I run a small restaurant that had to close because of the fires, will insurance cover lost income?
answer: If you have business interruption coverage (often part of a commercial policy), yes — it can cover lost net income and continuing expenses like payroll and rent while you're closed due to covered damage. File a claim with your commercial insurer immediately and gather profit/loss statements, tax returns, and payroll records. If insurance falls short, look into an SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loan at sba.gov/disaster, and the California Department of Insurance can help at 1-800-927-4357.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: usda help for farmers after wildfire
answer: Contact your local USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) office to apply for disaster programs like the Livestock Indemnity Program (LIP), Emergency Livestock Assistance Program (ELAP), Tree Assistance Program (TAP), and the Noninsured Crop Disaster Assistance Program (NAP). You can also apply for FSA Emergency Loans for physical and production losses. Find your local office at farmers.gov/recover.

question: how do i help my kid she wont talk since we lost the house
answer: Children often go quiet or regress after a disaster — it's a common stress response. The Disaster Distress Helpline (1-800-985-5990) can guide parents, and the National Child Traumatic Stress Network (nctsn.org) has free resources for talking with kids. Your county behavioral health department offers free children's crisis counseling through FEMA's Crisis Counseling Program when a disaster is declared. If she shows signs of self-harm or won't eat, call 988 or her pediatrician right away.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: can i clean mould myself or do i need a professionel
answer: For small areas (under ~10 sq ft), you can usually clean it yourself using detergent and water, wearing an N95 mask, gloves, and goggles. For larger areas, HVAC contamination, or if anyone in the home has asthma or a weakened immune system, hire a licensed mold remediation professional. In California, check contractor licenses at CSLB.ca.gov before hiring to avoid post-disaster scams.

question: i alredy went to dmv 3 weeks ago and still no license what now
answer: DMV says cards usually arrive in 3–4 weeks, so you're right at the edge. Check the status at dmv.ca.gov under "Driver's License & ID Card Status" using your info — that often tells you if it's been mailed. If it's been 60 days with nothing, call DMV at 1-800-777-0133. Your temporary paper license from the office visit is still valid to drive in the meantime.

question: i have a farm that got damaged who do i call
answer: Farms generally aren't eligible for SBA disaster loans — instead, contact your local USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) office or visit farmers.gov/recover. The FSA offers emergency loans, the Emergency Conservation Program, and Livestock Indemnity Program. You can also apply to FEMA for damage to your home, and check with the CA Department of Food and Agriculture for state-level help.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: am i eligable for fema if i rent
answer: Yes — renters can absolutely qualify for FEMA assistance. You can receive grants for temporary housing, replacement of essential personal property (clothing, furniture, appliances), medical/dental costs, and other disaster-related expenses not covered by insurance. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: My elderly father doesn't use computers and lost his job cleaning at a hotel that closed after the flood. How can he apply without going online?
answer: He can apply by phone — call EDD at 1-800-300-5616, Monday–Friday 8 a.m.–5 p.m. Pacific. A representative will take his application over the phone. He can also visit a Local Assistance Center or Disaster Recovery Center, where staff help in person with DUA, FEMA, and other recovery applications. Call 211 to find the nearest one.

question: sba loan max for homeowners
answer: Homeowners can borrow up to $500,000 from the SBA to repair or replace their primary residence, plus up to $100,000 for personal property like furniture, clothing, and vehicles. Secondary homes don't qualify. Apply at sba.gov/disaster.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: whats the difference between fema and sba loans do i need both
answer: FEMA grants don't have to be repaid but cover limited needs. If FEMA refers you to the SBA, fill out the SBA disaster loan application even if you don't want a loan — it's required to be considered for additional FEMA assistance like personal property and transportation help. If SBA denies you, FEMA may then provide more grant aid. Apply at sba.gov/disaster or call 1-800-659-2955.

question: does dmv waive the fee for replacment license if i lost it in a disater
answer: Yes — when the Governor declares a state of emergency, the DMV typically waives fees for replacement driver's licenses and ID cards for residents in the affected area. Tell the DMV staff your address was in the disaster zone when you apply. You can start the application at dmv.ca.gov and finish at a DMV office.

question: small business burned down can i get a loan
answer: Yes — the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) offers low-interest disaster loans for businesses of all sizes, including physical damage loans (up to $2 million) and Economic Injury Disaster Loans for lost revenue. Apply at sba.gov/disaster or call 1-800-659-2955. You should also register with FEMA, and check with your county for local business recovery resources.

question: How do I find out which hospitals are open after the wildfire?
answer: Call 211 or check your county public health department's website for current hospital and clinic status — they post closures and diversions during disasters. Local news and the county Office of Emergency Services also share updates. If you have a medical emergency, still call 911 — dispatchers will route you to the nearest operating facility.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: what if fema denied my vehicle request can i appeal
answer: Yes, you have 60 days from the date of your FEMA decision letter to appeal. Write a signed letter explaining why you disagree, include your FEMA registration number, and attach supporting documents — title, registration, insurance denial, repair estimate, and proof the vehicle was your primary transportation. Submit through DisasterAssistance.gov, by fax, or by mail to the address on your letter. You can also call 1-800-621-3362 for help with the appeal.
topic: Replacing a car or vehicle damaged in disaster

question: we own a small farm and lost barns and equipment in the fire, does the debris program cover agricultural buildings?
answer: The state debris removal program typically covers residential structures, but coverage for agricultural outbuildings, barns, and equipment varies by disaster declaration. Commercial and ag properties sometimes need to use the private property debris removal (alternative) route, with cleanup costs potentially reimbursable through SBA disaster loans or crop/farm insurance. Contact your county Ag Commissioner and CalRecycle for guidance specific to your disaster.

question: Can renters apply for FEMA assistance, or is that only for homeowners?
answer: Yes, renters can absolutely apply for FEMA assistance. FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) can provide rental assistance for temporary housing and money to replace essential personal property like clothing, furniture, and appliances. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA app, or by calling 1-800-621-3362. Renters can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans to replace personal property.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: How do I document earthquake damage for my insurance claim?
answer: Before cleaning up or throwing anything away, take photos and videos of every damaged area — walls, foundation, chimney, broken belongings, and the exterior. Make a written list of damaged items with approximate values and purchase dates if possible. Save receipts for any emergency repairs or temporary lodging. Then contact your earthquake insurer (usually CEA through your home insurer) to start the claim as soon as possible.

question: do i need to file with my insurance before fema will help with housing
answer: Yes — if you have homeowners or renters insurance, file a claim first. FEMA can't duplicate what insurance covers, but they may help with needs your policy doesn't cover (like Additional Living Expenses being delayed or exhausted). Send FEMA your insurance settlement or denial letter so they can review you for housing assistance. You can still register with FEMA right away while your claim is pending.

question: i called my pharmacy yesterday for an emergency refill but they said no, what now
answer: Try a different pharmacy in the same chain, or ask them specifically about California's emergency refill provisions during a declared disaster (pharmacists can dispense up to a 30-day supply of most non-controlled meds). If that fails, call your doctor's office or a telehealth service for a new prescription, or visit a Disaster Recovery Center or local urgent care. 211 can also locate free disaster medical clinics in your area.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: How does workers' compensation work if I was injured during a wildfire cleanup job?
answer: If you're an employee doing cleanup or rebuild work, your employer must carry workers' comp insurance and cover medical treatment plus lost wages for any on-the-job injury. Report the injury to your employer within 30 days and request a DWC-1 claim form. If your employer is unlicensed or uninsured, you can still file through the Uninsured Employers Benefits Trust Fund. Report unsafe conditions to Cal/OSHA at 1-833-579-0927.
topic: Workers' comp and job protection during evacuation

question: do i need insurance to apply
answer: No, you don't need insurance to apply for FEMA. But if you do have insurance, file that claim first — FEMA only covers losses your insurance doesn't. You can apply to FEMA at the same time at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: dua phone number spanish
answer: Call EDD at 1-800-300-5616 — they have English and Spanish service, Monday–Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Pacific Time. Free interpreter services are also available at that same number.

question: does fema pay you back for food that spoild when the power went out
answer: Unfortunately no — FEMA's Serious Needs Assistance is not a reimbursement for spoiled food or lost power. It's an upfront emergency payment for essentials like food, water, and medication going forward. You can still apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 if you have other disaster-related needs.

question: can i use sba loan money to pay off my old busines debts
answer: No, EIDL funds cannot be used to refinance existing long-term debt, expand your business, buy fixed assets, pay dividends/bonuses, or repay loans to stockholders. They can be used for working capital like rent, utilities, health benefits, and regular fixed debt payments that came due because of the disaster. If you have physical damage, a separate SBA Physical Disaster Loan covers repairs and replacement.

question: Hi, I'm a small almond grower in Fresno County and we lost a lot of trees in the storms and flooding this winter. What kind of disaster assistance can I actually apply for as a farmer?
answer: I'm sorry for your losses. As an orchard owner, you may qualify for the USDA Tree Assistance Program (TAP), which helps replant or rehabilitate damaged trees, and the Noninsured Crop Disaster Assistance Program (NAP) if your crop wasn't covered by federal crop insurance. FSA Emergency Loans can also cover physical damage and lost production. Call or visit your local USDA Farm Service Agency office in Fresno to start an application, and bring records of your losses, photos, and production history.

question: what if i already filed with CEA but havent heard back
answer: CEA claims are handled by your residential insurance company (the one that sold you the policy), not CEA directly. If it's been more than a few days, call your insurance agent and ask for your claim number and adjuster's contact. If you're not getting responses, you can file a complaint with the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357 or insurance.ca.gov. Keep written records of every call.

question: hotel said they dont take fema vouchers what do i do
answer: FEMA doesn't issue paper vouchers — under the Transitional Sheltering Assistance (TSA) program, FEMA pays participating hotels directly, and you can find the list of approved hotels by calling 1-800-621-3362 or checking your DisasterAssistance.gov account. If you booked elsewhere, save your receipts and apply for Lodging Expense Reimbursement instead. Call FEMA's helpline to be added to TSA or find a participating hotel near you.

question: hi so my apartment in altadena got smoke damage from the fires and my landlord is saying i still have to pay full rent even though i can't live there right now is that legal?
answer: In California, if a rental unit is uninhabitable due to a disaster, you generally do not owe rent for the period you can't live there. Under Civil Code 1942, tenants can withhold rent or repair-and-deduct in some habitability cases. Document the damage with photos, send your landlord a written notice, and contact Disaster Legal Services through 211 or Legal Aid for free help. You may also qualify for FEMA rental assistance at 1-800-621-3362 to cover temporary housing.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: is there a deadline for sba loans too
answer: Yes. SBA usually sets a 60-day deadline for physical damage loan applications and a 9-month deadline for Economic Injury Disaster Loans after the declaration date. Exact dates vary by disaster — check sba.gov/disaster or call 1-800-659-2955. Apply early; you can decline the loan later if you don't need it.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: do i have to use the appeal form fema sent or can i just write a letter
answer: You don't have to use the form — a written letter works fine. Just make sure it explains why you disagree with FEMA's decision and includes any supporting documents. Write your FEMA application number and the disaster number on every page so nothing gets lost.

question: How long does it typically take to get a rebuild permit approved after a wildfire in California?
answer: Timelines vary by jurisdiction, but expedited disaster rebuild permits in California often take 4–12 weeks once you submit complete plans, compared to 6+ months in normal times.
