Delays usually come from incomplete plans, septic/well review, or hillside grading issues. To speed things up, use your local Disaster Recovery Permit Center and consider hiring an architect familiar with post-fire rebuilds. Check your county's recovery website for current processing times.
topic: Long-term recovery: rebuilding permits and zoning

question: Are there free counseling services for children affected by California wildfires?
answer: Yes. FEMA's Crisis Counseling Assistance and Training Program (CCP) funds free, confidential counseling for disaster survivors including children, often delivered through county behavioral health departments. You can also call the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 (24/7, multilingual) or dial 211 to be connected with local children's mental health resources. California's CalHOPE program (calhope.org) specifically offers free disaster-related emotional support.
topic: Emotional support for children after a disaster

question: Is it safe to go back to my property after the fire?
answer: Wait until local officials officially announce that your area is safe to re-enter — fires can leave hazards like unstable structures, hot spots, and toxic ash. When you do return, wear an N95 mask, gloves, long sleeves, and sturdy boots. Don't turn on utilities yourself; if the fire department shut off your gas, water, or electricity, only utility crews should restore them.

question: can fema help my small business
answer: No, FEMA does not provide assistance for small businesses. You'll need to apply with the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) instead. SBA offers low-interest disaster loans for both physical damage and economic injury. Call the SBA Disaster Assistance Customer Service Center at 800-659-2955 or apply online at sba.gov/disaster.

question: I'm an 80 year old widow and a man knocked on my door saying he'd haul away my burned debris for $5000 cash, is this legit?
answer: This sounds like a scam — please do not pay or sign anything. Legitimate state debris removal is free to homeowners through the CalRecycle program, and reputable contractors never demand large cash payments door-to-door. Report this person to the Contractors State License Board at 1-800-321-2752 and to local law enforcement. If you'd like help, call 211 to connect with a recovery case manager.

question: How much money does FEMA actually give you?
answer: It varies based on your verified losses. FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) can provide funds for temporary housing, home repairs, and other serious disaster-related needs like medical, dental, childcare, and replacement of essential items. Awards are not loans and don't have to be repaid. The maximum changes each year — check your decision letter for your specific award.

question: where do i find a shelter near me
answer: Call 211 (or visit 211.org) to be connected to the nearest open disaster shelter. You can also text your ZIP code to 43362 (4FEMA) to find open shelters, or check the Red Cross shelter map at redcross.org/shelter. If you're in immediate danger, call 911.

question: right of entry form deadline
answer: Right-of-Entry (ROE) form deadlines are set by your county after each disaster, usually 30–60 days after the program opens. Submitting the ROE lets state crews access your property to remove debris at no out-of-pocket cost. Contact your county's disaster recovery website or call 211 to confirm the current deadline for your area.

question: do i need to file with insurance befor fema
answer: Yes — FEMA requires you to file with your insurance first, because FEMA cannot duplicate benefits your insurance covers. Go ahead and apply to FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 at the same time, but send FEMA your insurance settlement or denial letter once you have it. FEMA may help with uninsured or underinsured losses after your insurance pays out.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: where can i find a food bank near me
answer: Call 2-1-1 or visit 211ca.org to find the closest food bank or pantry. You can also use the California Association of Food Banks locator at cafoodbanks.org/find-food. Most food banks don't require ID, proof of income, or immigration status to receive free groceries.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: i already reported my outage yesterday but still nothing what now
answer: After major disasters, crews often have to repair transmission lines and substations before individual neighborhoods come back online, so it can take longer than usual. Call your utility again to confirm they have your address flagged (especially if your neighbors have power but you don't — that may mean a separate service line issue). PG&E: 1-800-743-5002, SCE: 1-800-611-1911, SDG&E: 1-800-411-7343.

question: How can I find out when my electricity will be restored after the wildfire?
answer: Check your utility's online outage map for an estimated restoration time: PG&E (pge.com/outages), SCE (sce.com/outages), or SDG&E (sdge.com/outages). After major disasters, restoration times can change as crews assess damage. You can also sign up for text/email alerts through your utility account.

question: Can I stay with family and still get FEMA money?
answer: Yes. FEMA's Displacement Assistance is flexible — you can use it whether you're in a hotel, staying with family or friends, or any other housing arrangement. You don't have to provide hotel receipts for Displacement Assistance, though Rental Assistance and Lodging Expense Reimbursement do require documentation. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.

question: is drinking water safe after the fire
answer: Don't drink tap water until your local water utility confirms it's safe — wildfires can damage pipes and cause benzene contamination. Check your water provider's website or call them directly. Boil-water notices and Do Not Drink advisories are common after fires. Free bottled water is usually distributed at Local Assistance Centers, evacuation shelters, and through 2-1-1 referrals.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: cant stop crying since the fire what do i do
answer: What you're feeling is a normal reaction to a very abnormal event. Please call the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 (or text the same number) — it's free, confidential, and available 24/7. You can also dial 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline anytime. If you're in immediate danger, call 911.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: Will my phone company give me a credit for the days service was out after the wildfire?
answer: Often yes. California requires telecom providers to offer bill credits and waive certain fees during declared disasters. Contact your provider directly and ask for a disaster-related service credit, then keep records. If they refuse or you have trouble, file a complaint with the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) at cpuc.ca.gov/consumer-support or call 1-800-649-7570.

question: im undocumented and scared to ask for mental health help for my kids after the fire, is it safe
answer: Yes — mental health and crisis counseling services do not ask about immigration status, and FEMA's Crisis Counseling Program is available to everyone regardless of status. The Disaster Distress Helpline (1-800-985-5990, press 2 for Spanish) is free, confidential, anonymous, and multilingual. Community clinics, school counselors, and 211 can also connect your children to free support without immigration questions. Your kids' wellbeing comes first, and reaching out is safe.
topic: Emotional support for children after a disaster

question: how long does FEMA aproval take for housing
answer: After you apply, FEMA usually schedules a home inspection within a few days (for damaged homes) and makes a decision within about 7–10 days, though it can take longer in large disasters. Check status anytime at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. If you need shelter right now, don't wait — call 211 for emergency housing while your application is reviewed.

question: i applied for unemployment but got denied does that mean no dua either
answer: Not necessarily — getting denied for regular UI is often the first step toward qualifying for DUA. EDD should automatically review your claim for DUA if your area has a presidential disaster declaration. If you haven't heard about DUA, call EDD at 1-800-300-5616 and specifically ask them to evaluate your claim for Disaster Unemployment Assistance.

question: i applied 3 weeks ago and havent heard anything is that normal
answer: Yes, that's within the normal range — SBA disaster loan decisions typically take 2-4 weeks once your application is complete, though it can be longer in major disasters. Log into the MySBA Loan Portal at sba.gov to check your status, or call SBA's Disaster Customer Service at 1-800-659-2955. Make sure they have all requested documents — missing paperwork is the most common delay.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: do i need to bring anything to apply for calfresh
answer: Helpful documents include a photo ID, Social Security numbers for household members applying, proof of income (pay stubs), rent/mortgage and utility bills, and proof of any disaster-related expenses. But don't delay applying if you've lost paperwork in the disaster — you can submit documents later or sign sworn statements. Apply at GetCalFresh.org, BenefitsCal.com, or by calling your county office.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: what if i already applied to fema as a renter but they denied me
answer: Don't give up — many renters are initially denied for fixable reasons like missing documents or identity verification. You have 60 days from the decision letter to appeal in writing. Include a signed letter explaining why you disagree and any supporting documents (lease, receipts, photos). Submit through your DisasterAssistance.gov account, by mail, or by fax. Free help with appeals is available through Disaster Legal Services — call 211 or FEMA at 1-800-621-3362.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: Hi, I'm really overwhelmed. We lost everything in the fire and I haven't even thought about taxes. Do I need to do anything special with the IRS?
answer: First, take a breath — the IRS has automatic relief for disaster victims, so you don't need to file anything immediately to get an extension. If your address is in the FEMA-declared disaster area, filing and payment deadlines are postponed automatically. You can also claim your uninsured disaster losses as a casualty loss on either this year's or last year's return (whichever gives you a bigger refund). Call the IRS disaster hotline at 1-866-562-5227 if you need help.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: I'm undocumented and afraid to go to a shelter but my dog needs care after smoke inhalation, is there somewhere safe?
answer: You will not be asked about immigration status at disaster shelters or animal services — they are open to everyone. For your dog, contact your local Humane Society, SPCA, or county Animal Services; many offer free emergency vet care for disaster-affected pets, no questions asked. RedRover Relief (redrover.org) also provides urgent vet care grants. Call 2-1-1 confidentially for a referral to the closest free clinic.

question: Is there a deadline to register with FEMA?
answer: Yes — typically 60 days from the date the disaster is declared, though deadlines are sometimes extended. Check the specific deadline for your disaster at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362. Don't wait — register as soon as you safely can.

question: I'm 78 and live alone in Napa. The earthquake broke a lot of things in my house and I'm scared. Who can help me clean up?
answer: You're not alone — help is available. Call 211 (free, 24/7) and tell them you're a senior who needs cleanup and recovery assistance; they can connect you with local volunteer groups, the Red Cross, and senior services. The Red Cross (1-800-733-2767) often provides cleanup kits and welfare checks. If a federal disaster has been declared, FEMA's Disaster Case Management can assign someone to help walk you through recovery — call 1-800-621-3362.

question: I'm undocumented and lost all my papers in the flood. Is it safe for me to go to the county office to get my kids' birth certificates replaced?
answer: Yes — county recorder offices issue birth certificates regardless of the parent's immigration status, and they do not share information with immigration enforcement. If your children were born in California, you can request their certified birth certificates from the county recorder where they were born, or from CA Vital Records (cdph.ca.gov). FEMA also has disaster assistance available for U.S. citizen children even if parents are undocumented — call 1-800-621-3362. For free legal help, contact 211 or CHIRLA at 1-888-624-4752.

question: earthquake just hit what do i do first
answer: First, check yourself and others for injuries — call 911 for medical emergencies. Stay alert for aftershocks, and if you smell gas or see damage to gas lines, shut off the gas at the meter. Do not re-enter damaged buildings until local officials say it's safe. Call 211 for shelter, food, and disaster relief info.

question: i applied for the sba loan 3 weeks ago and havent heard anything what do i do
answer: That's within the normal review window, but you can check your status anytime by logging into your SBA disaster loan account at sba.gov/disaster or by calling the Customer Service Center at 800-659-2955. After your application is submitted, SBA usually sends an inspector to estimate damages, which can add time. Have your application number ready when you call.

question: how do i get rental assistance from fema
answer: Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov, on the FEMA mobile app, or call 1-800-621-3362. If approved, FEMA sends Rental Assistance as a lump sum to cover temporary rent (and deposit/utilities) while your home is being repaired. You'll need to show you used the money for housing and can request continued rental assistance every 1–3 months if you still need it.

question: how do i report an unlicensed contractor
answer: Report unlicensed contractors to the Contractors State License Board (CSLB) at 1-800-321-2752 or through the Disaster Help Center at cslb.ca.gov/Media_Room/Disaster_Help_Center. If you saw them working at a job site, use the 'Report Unlawful Activity' link. If you hired them, file a 'Licensed and Unlicensed Project Complaint.' Reports can be anonymous.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: my teenager is acting out and angry since we lost our home, is this from the trama
answer: Yes — anger, irritability, and acting out are common trauma responses in teens after losing a home. Let them know their feelings are valid, keep listening without judgment, maintain routines, and watch for warning signs like substance use or talk of self-harm. Free help is available: call or text the Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990, or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline if you're worried about their safety. CalHOPE also has peer support tailored to teens.
topic: Emotional support for children after a disaster

question: Hi, I own a small bakery in Altadena and we had to close for weeks because of the fires and evacuations. We didn't have direct damage but we lost a ton of business. Is there anything I can apply for?
answer: Yes — you may qualify for an SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL), which is designed exactly for situations like yours, where a business in a declared disaster area can't meet its normal operating expenses. EIDL funds can cover working capital like rent, utilities, payroll, and fixed debts. The first payment is deferred 12 months with no interest accruing during that time, and the interest rate is capped at 4%. Apply online at sba.gov/disaster or call 800-659-2955.

question: what if i already applied to fema but havent heard anything
answer: Log in to your account at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362 to check your application status. FEMA usually schedules a home inspection within a couple of weeks of applying, and decisions come by mail or through your online account. If you've been waiting more than a few weeks with no contact, call them directly — sometimes missing documents or an unverified identity is holding things up.

question: Hi, our basement and first floor got flooded last week and we have an NFIP policy through our mortgage, I've never filed a claim before and I'm honestly really overwhelmed, where do I even begin?
answer: Take a breath — here's the order: 1) Call your flood insurance agent or carrier now to report the loss and get a claim number. 2) Before throwing anything out, photograph and video every damaged room and item. 3) Make a written inventory with descriptions and approximate values. 4) An adjuster will be assigned to inspect — you can start safe cleanup and save damaged samples (like carpet swatches). For questions about NFIP, call 1-877-336-2627.

question: hi so my small bakery burned down in the wildfire and i'm trying to figure out if i can get an sba loan to cover my lost income while we rebuild, is that a thing?
answer: Yes — SBA offers Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) to help small businesses cover operating expenses (payroll, rent, bills) they could have met if the disaster hadn't happened. You can also apply for a Business Physical Disaster Loan to repair or replace the building and equipment. Start at sba.gov/disaster or call 1-800-659-2955 to apply.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: where do i take my horses to evacuate
answer: Contact your county Animal Services or fairgrounds — many California fairgrounds (like Pomona, Ventura, and Del Mar) open as large animal evacuation sites during disasters. Call 211 for current shelter locations in your area, and check your county Office of Emergency Services social media for real-time updates. If you can't trailer them yourself, county animal control and groups like the Humane Society or local CART (County Animal Response Teams) can help with rescue.
topic: Livestock and large animal evacuation and recovery

question: Does FEMA pay for a hotel if my house is unlivable?
answer: Yes. FEMA's Lodging Expense Reimbursement can reimburse you for hotel or motel costs while you're displaced, and Displacement Assistance provides upfront money you can use for a hotel, to stay with family, or other housing. You must apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362, and save all your receipts. This is only available if your home is in a federally declared disaster area.

question: How much does it cost to get well water tested after a flood in California?
answer: A basic bacterial test (total coliform/E. coli) typically runs $30–$75 through a state-certified lab. Tests for chemicals, nitrates, or heavy metals cost more. After a federally declared disaster, some counties offer free or reduced-cost testing — check with your county environmental health department or call 211. The State Water Resources Control Board keeps a list of certified labs (ELAP) on its website.

question: do i have to file with insuance first before fema will help with my truck
answer: Yes — FEMA is the payer of last resort, so you need to file with your auto insurance first (comprehensive coverage typically covers fire, flood, and falling debris). Once you have a settlement or denial letter, submit it to FEMA. If insurance doesn't fully cover the loss or you were uninsured, FEMA's Transportation Assistance or an SBA disaster loan may help fill the gap.
topic: Replacing a car or vehicle damaged in disaster

question: Does FEMA cover livestock losses from a wildfire?
answer: FEMA's Individual Assistance generally does not cover livestock losses, but the USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) does through the Livestock Indemnity Program (LIP) for animals killed by disaster, and the Emergency Livestock Assistance Program (ELAP) for feed, water, and transport losses. Contact your local FSA county office within 30 days of the loss and document deaths with photos, vet records, and inventory lists. California ranchers may also qualify for SBA disaster loans for damaged barns, fencing, and equipment.
topic: Livestock and large animal evacuation and recovery

question: Hi, my family just lost everything in the wildfire and I honestly don't even know where to start, can you walk me through the steps?
answer: I'm so sorry you're going through this. Here's a basic roadmap: (1) Get to safety and call 211 for shelter, food, and local resources. (2) Contact your insurance company to open a claim. (3) Apply for FEMA assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 — this can cover temporary housing and other needs. (4) Once your area is cleared, sign up for CalRecycle's debris removal program (usually free for eligible homeowners). (5) Visit a Local Assistance Center if one opens in your area — they bring all the agencies together in one place.

question: fema denied me how do i appeal
answer: You have 60 days from the date on your FEMA decision letter to appeal. Read the letter carefully — it tells you exactly what documents FEMA needs (like repair estimates, receipts, or proof of ownership). Submit your appeal online at DisasterAssistance.gov, by mail to FEMA at P.O. Box 10055, Hyattsville, MD 20782-8055, by fax to (800) 827-8112, or in person at a Disaster Recovery Center. Call 1-800-621-3362 if you need help.

question: I'm an undocumented mom and I'm scared to enroll my kids in a new school while ours is closed, is it safe?
answer: Yes — California public schools must enroll all children regardless of immigration status, and schools are not allowed to ask about or share immigration information. Displaced students have the right to immediate enrollment under the McKinney-Vento Act, even without records or proof of address. Contact the district's homeless/displaced student liaison for help getting your kids placed quickly.

question: what if i already filed the claim but the adjuster hasnt come out yet
answer: That's common after major floods when adjusters are backed up. In the meantime: keep documenting damage with photos/video, save receipts for any emergency repairs or temporary lodging, and don't throw out damaged items until the adjuster sees them (or keep samples). If it's been more than a couple weeks with no contact, call your insurance carrier directly and ask for a status update and your adjuster's name and number.

question: hi my house burned down in the fire and i don't even know where to start, what do i do first?
answer: I'm so sorry you're going through this. First, if you have insurance, file a claim with them right away — FEMA needs that info. Then register with FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362. Take photos of the damage and make a list of what you lost. FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) can help with temporary housing, repairs, and other serious needs.

question: What classification of contractor license do I need to look for when rebuilding my home after a wildfire?
answer: For a full home rebuild, hire a licensed General Building Contractor (Class B). Specialty work like roofing (C-39), electrical (C-10), or plumbing (C-36) requires the matching specialty classification. Verify the classification matches the work on CSLB's License Check tool, and make sure the license is active with workers' comp coverage.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: how do i start a flood insurance claim
answer: Contact your flood insurance agent or carrier as soon as possible to file a Notice of Loss. Before cleaning up, take photos and videos of all damage and make a list of damaged items with their value. For NFIP-specific help, call 1-877-336-2627 or visit floodsmart.gov/recover.

question: Does standard homeowners insurance cover earthquake damage in California?
answer: No. Standard homeowners and renters policies in California do not cover earthquake damage. You need a separate earthquake policy, most commonly through the California Earthquake Authority (CEA) via your existing insurer. If you have a CEA policy, contact your insurance agent right away to start a claim. If you're uninsured, you may still qualify for FEMA assistance if a federal disaster is declared — apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.

question: i submitted my appeal like 3 weeks ago and havent heard anything is that normal
answer: Yes, that's within the normal window. FEMA usually decides appeals within 30 days but it can take up to 90 days. You can check the status by logging into your DisasterAssistance.gov account or calling the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362. If they need more info from you, they'll reach out — so keep an eye on your mail and account messages.

question: so i own a small food truck and i couldnt operate after the fires shut down the area do i count as self employed for DUA
answer: Yes — small business owners and self-employed people like food truck operators are exactly who DUA is designed to help when regular UI isn't an option. Apply through myEDD or call 1-800-300-5616. Have your business records, tax returns (Schedule C or SE), and any documentation showing your truck couldn't operate due to the disaster.

question: replace social security card
answer: Request a free replacement Social Security card at ssa.gov/myaccount (most people can do it fully online) or call 1-800-772-1213. If you can't use the online service, visit your local SSA office — you can find it at ssa.gov/locator. You'll need some form of identity proof, but SSA can work with you if your ID was destroyed in the disaster.

question: do renters qualify for sba loans
answer: Yes — renters can apply for an SBA disaster loan of up to $100,000 to replace personal property damaged or destroyed in a declared disaster (clothing, furniture, appliances, vehicles, etc.). You don't have to own a home or business. Apply at sba.gov/disaster.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: how long does debre removal take after i sign the form
answer: Once you submit your Right-of-Entry form, it typically takes several weeks to a few months before crews reach your property, depending on how many properties are in the queue and site accessibility. Phase 1 (household hazardous waste) usually happens first across the whole disaster area, then Phase 2 (structural debris) is scheduled property by property. Your county will notify you before crews arrive.

question: how long do i need to wait before testing my well after floodwaters reseed
answer: Wait until floodwaters have fully receded and the well has been disinfected (shock chlorinated), then flush the system until you no longer smell chlorine — usually a few days. Collect your water sample after that and send it to a state-certified lab. Don't drink the water until results come back clean for total coliform and E. coli. Your county environmental health office can walk you through the steps.

question: can i upload documents online instead of mailing
answer: Yes — uploading is the fastest way. Log into your account at DisasterAssistance.gov and use the Upload Center to send documents. Be sure your FEMA application number and disaster number are on every page. You can also fax to (800) 827-8112 or mail to FEMA, P.O. Box 10055, Hyattsville, MD 20782-8055.

question: car burned up in the fire can fema replace it
answer: FEMA may provide some assistance for vehicle repair or replacement under its Transportation Assistance category, but only if the vehicle was damaged by the disaster, you have no other working vehicle, and it's needed for daily use. First, file a claim with your auto insurance (comprehensive coverage usually covers fire). Then register with FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 or DisasterAssistance.gov. You can also apply for an SBA disaster loan to cover the gap.
topic: Replacing a car or vehicle damaged in disaster

question: i applied for fema but they want me to send id and i dont have any id anymore what do i do
answer: Tell FEMA — call 1-800-621-3362. FEMA can often verify your identity through other means (like answering security questions or using public records) so you don't get stuck. In the meantime, start replacing your ID: dmv.ca.gov for a driver's license/ID (fees often waived in disasters), and ssa.gov for a Social Security card. You can upload any documents you do gather to your account at DisasterAssistance.gov.

question: how do i prove i own my home if i lost the paperwork in the fire
answer: FEMA accepts many alternatives: property tax bills, mortgage statements, home insurance policies, a deed, or even a public official's letter. If those are gone too, you can submit a self-declarative statement as a last resort. County recorder offices can also provide copies of your deed. Call 1-800-621-3362 if you need guidance on what will work for your situation.

question: How do I claim a casualty loss for property destroyed in a California wildfire?
answer: File IRS Form 4684 (Casualties and Thefts) with your federal return to claim uninsured or unreimbursed disaster losses. Because California wildfires are federally declared disasters, you can choose to deduct the loss on the tax year the disaster happened OR amend the prior year's return for a faster refund. Keep records of property value, insurance payouts, and FEMA assistance. See IRS Publication 547 for details.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: what if my lot is now in a new flood zone after the fire, do i have to elevate when i rebuild
answer: Possibly yes. Post-fire watersheds often get remapped into higher flood or debris-flow risk zones, and if your property is now in a Special Flood Hazard Area, FEMA's NFIP 'substantial damage' rules require you to rebuild to current floodplain standards — which can mean elevating the structure. FloodSmart.gov's 'Rebuild Better' guidance explains the requirements. Check with your local floodplain administrator (usually at the city/county building department) before finalizing plans, since building noncompliant could make you ineligible for future flood insurance claims.
topic: Long-term recovery: rebuilding permits and zoning

question: can i rebuild bigger than my old house was
answer: Often yes — many California jurisdictions allow up to 10% additional square footage on a like-for-like rebuild without triggering full discretionary review, but anything beyond that usually requires standard planning approval and may need to meet current setback, height, and zoning rules. Coastal Zone, hillside, and WUI areas have extra restrictions. Ask your local planning department about their post-disaster rebuild ordinance before drawing up bigger plans.
topic: Long-term recovery: rebuilding permits and zoning

question: I'm undocumented but my kids are US citizens, can I still apply for FEMA?
answer: Yes. If at least one person in your household is a U.S. citizen, non-citizen national, or qualified non-citizen (including children with Social Security numbers), your household may apply for FEMA assistance. You can apply on behalf of your minor child. FEMA does not share immigration status info with ICE for assistance purposes.

question: i already called 211 but they just gave me a list i still feel awful
answer: I'm sorry — a list isn't always what you need in the moment. Try calling or texting the Disaster Distress Helpline directly at 1-800-985-5990; a real crisis counselor will talk with you right then, no appointment needed. If you'd like ongoing support, ask your county behavioral health department specifically about the FEMA Crisis Counseling Program — they assign counselors who follow up with you. And dial 988 anytime you feel unsafe.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: can i buy pet food with calfresh or is there help for that too
answer: CalFresh/EBT cannot be used for pet food. However, many food banks distribute free pet food, and organizations like the SPCA, Humane Society, and local animal shelters often run pet food pantries — especially after disasters. Call 2-1-1 to find pet food assistance in your area, and the Red Cross often includes pet supplies at disaster shelters.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: Can I get a passport replaced if it burned in the fire?
answer: Yes. Apply for a replacement at travel.state.gov by filing form DS-64 (report lost/stolen) and DS-11 (new application) at an acceptance facility, usually a post office or library. The standard fee is $130 plus a $35 execution fee. If you need it urgently for a disaster-related reason, request expedited service. The State Department occasionally waives fees for major disasters — ask when you apply.

question: who do i call about gas smell after earthquake
answer: Leave the area immediately, don't use any switches or phones inside, and once you're safely outside call 911 and your gas utility: PG&E 1-800-743-5000, SoCalGas 1-800-427-2200, or SDG&E 1-800-411-7343. Do not go back in until the utility says it's safe.

question: will i lose my house if i take out an sba disaster loan
answer: Not necessarily. Collateral is only required for SBA disaster loans over $50,000, and for loans of $200,000 or less, SBA will not require your primary residence as collateral if you have other assets of equal value. Real estate is the preferred collateral when it is required. You can discuss specifics with an SBA loan officer at 800-659-2955.

question: I'm undocumented and my family lost our apartment in the fire — can we still get any disaster help?
answer: You may still qualify. FEMA can provide assistance if at least one member of your household is a U.S. citizen, non-citizen national, or qualified non-citizen (this includes a child born in the U.S.). FEMA does not share immigration status with ICE. Even if you don't qualify for FEMA, you can get help from the Red Cross, 211, local nonprofits, and state programs regardless of status. Disaster legal aid is also free — call 211 to be referred.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: how long does it take to get a new license in the mail from dmv
answer: DMV says you should receive your new driver's license or ID card in the mail within 3 to 4 weeks after your office visit. If it hasn't arrived after 60 days, check status at dmv.ca.gov under "Driver's License & ID Card Status" or call 1-800-777-0133. The DMV will give you a temporary paper license to use in the meantime.

question: Does FEMA pay for mold removal after a disaster?
answer: FEMA doesn't have a dedicated 'mold' program, but its Clean and Sanitize assistance (part of Other Needs Assistance) provides a one-time payment to help prevent additional damage and health risks, which can include mold cleanup. Home Repair Assistance may also cover repairs to mold-damaged structural areas if the damage was caused by the declared disaster. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362, and document the damage with photos.

question: difference between flood insurance and homeowners
answer: Standard homeowners insurance does NOT cover flood damage from rising water, mudflow, or storm surge — you need a separate flood policy, usually through the NFIP. Homeowners typically covers wind, fire, and interior water damage from things like burst pipes. If you're unsure what you have, call your agent and ask specifically about flood coverage.

question: What is the maximum amount I can borrow from the SBA after a disaster?
answer: The maximum combined SBA disaster loan amount for a business is $2 million across both the Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) and the Physical Disaster Loan. The actual amount you're approved for depends on your demonstrated financial need and ability to repay. Loans over $50,000 require collateral. Apply at sba.gov/disaster or call 800-659-2955.

question: what if my insurance company is taking forever to respond
answer: Under California law, insurers must acknowledge your claim within 15 days and accept or deny it within 40 days of receiving proof of loss. If they're stalling, send a written follow-up, keep a log of every call (date, name, what was said), and file a complaint with the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357 or insurance.ca.gov. You can also request an advance payment for ALE and contents while the full claim is processed.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: daycare closed too what do i do
answer: FEMA's Other Needs Assistance can provide money for new or increased child care expenses caused by the disaster — apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362. The California Child Care Resource & Referral Network (rrnetwork.org or 1-800-543-7793) can help you find open licensed providers nearby. Call 211 for emergency child care resources in your county.

question: wheres the sba application
answer: Apply online at sba.gov/disaster — click "Apply for a disaster loan." You can also call 1-800-659-2955 (TTY 1-800-877-8339) or visit a local Disaster Recovery Center for in-person help. Have your insurance info, income documents, and property details ready.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: can small business owners get disaster help
answer: Yes. Small businesses can apply for SBA disaster loans at sba.gov/disaster — physical damage loans up to $2 million for repairs and Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) to cover operating expenses you can't meet because of the disaster. Call SBA at 1-800-659-2955 for help. Private nonprofits are also eligible.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: I'm 78 and lost my home in the Eaton fire. A man came to my door offering to clear debris cheap if I pay him half upfront in cash. My son is worried.
answer: Your son is right to be worried — this has all the warning signs of disaster fraud targeting seniors. Do NOT pay cash up front. In California, down payments are capped at 10% or $1,000, whichever is less. Ask for his license number and verify it at cslb.ca.gov, or call CSLB at 1-800-321-2752. If you qualify, the government-sponsored debris removal program may clear your lot at no out-of-pocket cost — check with your county.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: Where can I get a tetanus shot after cleaning up debris from my flooded house?
answer: Most urgent care clinics, county public health clinics, and many pharmacies (CVS, Walgreens) offer tetanus boosters as walk-ins. After a disaster, counties often set up free vaccination sites at Local Assistance Centers — call 211 to find one near you. A booster is recommended if your last shot was more than 5 years ago and you have a wound, or 10 years for routine protection.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: can FEMA help pay for earthquake damage if i dont have earthquake insurance
answer: Possibly. If the President declares a federal disaster for your area, FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) can provide grants for temporary housing, home repairs, and other serious needs not covered by insurance. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov, on the FEMA app, or by calling 1-800-621-3362. Note that FEMA assistance is typically less than full repair costs — you may also qualify for a low-interest SBA disaster loan.

question: can i get an sba loan if i alredy got fema money
answer: Yes. SBA disaster loans are designed to cover losses NOT fully covered by insurance or FEMA. In fact, FEMA often refers applicants to SBA first — if you're denied or under-funded by SBA, you may then qualify for additional FEMA grants. Applying for both is encouraged.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: How does an SBA disaster loan work for replacing a vehicle destroyed in a wildfire?
answer: The SBA offers low-interest disaster loans to homeowners and renters of up to $100,000 for personal property, which includes replacing a vehicle damaged or destroyed in a declared disaster. The vehicle must have been used for personal (not business) transportation and the loss must not be covered by insurance or FEMA. Apply at sba.gov/disaster after registering with FEMA. Business vehicles can be covered under a separate physical damage business loan up to $2 million.
topic: Replacing a car or vehicle damaged in disaster

question: how do i get the ash and debri cleaned up from my lot
answer: California has a state-run debris removal program through CalRecycle and Cal OES that's typically free to eligible homeowners after a major wildfire. You'll need to submit a Right-of-Entry (ROE) form through your county — watch for announcements from your local Public Works or Environmental Health department. Don't try to clean up wildfire ash yourself; it contains heavy metals and other toxic materials.

question: Will applying for disaster aid affect my green card application under the public charge rule?
answer: No. Disaster relief — including FEMA assistance, food banks, shelter, and Disaster Unemployment Assistance — is not counted under the public charge rule. USCIS has confirmed that emergency disaster relief does not affect green card or visa applications. You can safely seek help without immigration consequences.

question: Hi, I'm really shaken up — there was a big earthquake last night and my house has cracks in the walls and the chimney looks like it's leaning. I don't know if it's safe to stay. What should I do?
answer: I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Do not stay in the home if you see structural damage like a leaning chimney — that can collapse in an aftershock. Leave the building, turn off the gas if you smell any leak, and contact your local building department for a safety inspection (many cities offer free post-earthquake inspections). Call 211 to find emergency shelter, and start documenting damage with photos for your insurance claim.

question: how do i apply for fema
answer: You can apply for FEMA disaster assistance three ways: online at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA mobile app, or by calling 1-800-621-3362 (TTY 1-800-462-7585). Have your Social Security number, insurance info, address of the damaged property, and a description of damage ready. Apply as soon as possible after a disaster is declared in your area.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: What is the difference between regular unemployment and DUA?
answer: Regular Unemployment Insurance (UI) is for workers who lost W-2 jobs and have enough recent wages on file with EDD. Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) is a federal program that covers people who don't qualify for regular UI — like the self-employed, farmers, or those who just started a job — when a presidentially declared disaster causes them to lose work. EDD will first check if you qualify for regular UI; if not, they'll consider you for DUA.

question: power out how do i report
answer: Report the outage directly to your utility: PG&E at 1-800-743-5002, Southern California Edison at 1-800-611-1911, or SDG&E at 1-800-411-7343. You can also report and track outages on their websites or apps. If you see downed power lines, stay back and call 911.

question: How can I make sure my monetary donation actually goes to California wildfire survivors?
answer: Give to established organizations with a track record in California disaster response — examples include the California Community Foundation's Wildfire Recovery Fund, the American Red Cross, Direct Relief, and local community foundations in the affected county. Verify charities on CharityNavigator.org or the CA Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts before donating. Avoid donating through unsolicited social media posts or texts, which are often scams after disasters.

question: is my well water safe after the flood
answer: No — assume your private well is contaminated until tested. Boil water for drinking/cooking until you can disinfect the well and get it tested. Contact your local environmental health department for a list of state-certified labs, or call 211 for a referral. The CDC recommends testing for total coliform and E. coli before resuming use.

question: how do i no if my contracter is licensed for debri removal
answer: Use the CSLB "Check a License" tool at cslb.ca.gov or call 1-800-321-CSLB (2752). Contractors performing debris removal must hold a valid California license in the appropriate classification (typically a C-21 demolition or A general engineering license) and carry workers' comp insurance. If you suspect unlicensed work, report it to CSLB's Disaster Help Center.

question: hi my kids school burned down in the fire and i have no idea when they will go back or where, im freaking out about their education
answer: I'm so sorry you're going through this. Your school district will coordinate alternate locations or temporary campuses — contact the district office directly for placement info. The California Department of Education (cde.ca.gov) tracks disaster-affected schools and posts reopening updates. In the meantime, FEMA's Individuals and Households Program can help with child care costs caused by the disaster if you apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362.

question: How can I find out when my child's school will reopen after the wildfire?
answer: Reopening dates are set by your local school district based on building safety inspections and air quality. Check your district's website and sign up for their emergency alert system if available. The California Department of Education (cde.ca.gov) also posts statewide updates on disaster-impacted schools. Local news and 211 can also confirm reopening dates.

question: What is FEMA Displacement Assistance and how much is it?
answer: Displacement Assistance is a lump-sum payment from FEMA to help you pay for immediate housing — a hotel, staying with family, or any available option — when your home is unlivable due to a declared disaster. The amount is based on a 14-day local lodging rate for your household size. You can apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362, and it's separate from longer-term Rental Assistance.

question: I'm a renter in Altadena and lost everything in the fire, do I even have insurance options?
answer: If you had renters insurance, file a claim with that company right away — it should cover your personal belongings and Additional Living Expenses (ALE) for temporary housing. If you didn't have renters insurance, you're not out of options: apply to FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 for rental and personal property assistance, and consider an SBA disaster loan for renters at sba.gov/disaster. Local nonprofits and 211 can also connect you with immediate help.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: landlord wants to raise rent after fire repairs
answer: After a state of emergency is declared, California's anti-price-gouging law (Penal Code 396) caps rent increases at 10% above pre-disaster rent for at least 30 days, and often longer when extended by the Governor. Raising rent above that, or evicting to re-rent at a higher price, is illegal. Report violations to the California Attorney General at oag.ca.gov or your local DA's office.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: what if i already applied but havent heard back
answer: FEMA typically responds within about 10 days after a home inspection. Check your status anytime by logging in at DisasterAssistance.gov or calling 1-800-621-3362. Make sure FEMA has your current phone number and address, and watch for letters or calls from inspectors — missing one can delay your case.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: can i use my ebt card if i lost food in the power outage
answer: Yes — if you lost food due to a power outage or disaster, you can request CalFresh replacement benefits. Report the loss to your county social services office within 10 days of the disaster. You'll need to fill out a CF 303 form stating what was lost. Some counties allow mass replacements after declared disasters without individual forms.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: insurance adjuster lowballed me what do i do
answer: You don't have to accept the first offer. Get your own repair estimates from licensed contractors, document why the adjuster's figures are too low, and submit a written request for re-inspection or reconsideration. You can also hire a public adjuster (who works for you, not the insurer) or file a complaint with the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357. For large losses, a disaster insurance attorney may also help — many offer free consultations.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: Hi, my family and I just evacuated and we're sitting in our car in a parking lot. We have nowhere to go tonight and a little money but not enough for a hotel, what do we do?
answer: I'm sorry you're going through this. First, call 211 right now — they can direct you to the nearest open emergency shelter that has space tonight and can sometimes arrange transportation. If a federal disaster has been declared, apply for FEMA assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 and ask about Displacement Assistance, which is upfront money you can use for a hotel. The American Red Cross (1-800-733-2767) also opens shelters during California disasters.

question: Does California's Franchise Tax Board also extend state tax deadlines after a disaster?
answer: Yes. The California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) typically conforms to IRS disaster relief and extends state filing and payment deadlines to match. For the 2025 wildfires, the FTB postponed California state tax deadlines to October 15, 2025 for affected counties. Check ftb.ca.gov/disaster for the latest list of covered counties and deadlines.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: I'm undocumented and renting in LA county, my place flooded — can I still get help without risking anything?
answer: Yes, you have rights regardless of immigration status. California law protects all tenants, and your landlord cannot retaliate or threaten to report you. While FEMA cash assistance requires a household member with eligible immigration status (a U.S. citizen child counts), you can access Red Cross aid, local nonprofit help, food, shelter, and Disaster Legal Services without any status check. Call 211 for confidential local resources, and contact CHIRLA or a local immigrant rights group for tenant help.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: how much downpayment can a contracter legaly ask for in califrnia
answer: Under California law, a contractor cannot ask for more than 10% of the total contract price OR $1,000 — whichever is LESS — as a down payment. Anyone demanding more is violating the law. Report them to CSLB at 1-800-321-CSLB (2752) or through the Disaster Help Center at cslb.ca.gov.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: my dad uses oxygen at home and the power is out where can we go
answer: Go to a county-designated Medical Shelter or a Care and Reception Center — call 211 right now and tell them he's oxygen-dependent, they'll direct you to the closest one. Many utilities (PG&E, SCE, SDG&E) also run Community Resource Centers with power during outages. If his oxygen runs low before you get there, call 911 — they can transport and provide oxygen.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: how long is the tax extention for california wildfire victims
answer: For taxpayers affected by the January 2025 California wildfires, the IRS postponed various federal tax deadlines until October 15, 2025. This covers individual returns, business returns, quarterly estimated payments, and payroll tax deposits originally due during the relief period. Check IRS notice CA-2025-01 at irs.gov for the full list.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: What's the deadline to file a Proof of Loss with NFIP?
answer: Under standard NFIP rules, you must submit a signed and sworn Proof of Loss within 60 days of the flood, though FEMA frequently extends this deadline after major disasters. Your adjuster usually helps prepare it, but the policyholder is ultimately responsible for filing it. Check with your carrier or floodsmart.gov for any current extensions tied to your disaster declaration.

question: do i need a permit to rebuild my house after the fire
answer: Yes, you'll need building permits from your local city or county planning department before rebuilding. Many California jurisdictions have set up expedited 'one-stop' permit centers after recent disasters (like the LA County Rebuild Permitting Office for fire survivors). Contact your local building department to ask about fee waivers and streamlined review for disaster rebuilds. Call 211 if you need help finding your local permit office.
topic: Long-term recovery: rebuilding permits and zoning

question: hi my husband doesn't have papers but i'm a citizen and our kids too, we lost everything in the fire, can we still apply for fema without putting him at risk?
answer: Yes — as a U.S. citizen you can apply for FEMA for your household, and your citizen children also qualify. FEMA does not share applicant information with immigration enforcement for the purpose of immigration action. Only list yourself or your kids as the applicant; your husband's status does not need to be disclosed. You can register at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362.

question: how do i check if a contractor is licensed in ca
answer: Use the CSLB's free 'Check a License' tool at cslb.ca.gov. You can search by license number, business name, or personal name to verify the license is active, in the right classification, and has workers' comp insurance. Never hire anyone who can't show you a valid license — unlicensed contractors are common after disasters.
topic: Contractor licensing and avoiding post-disaster fraud

question: I'm undocumented and I got burned helping a neighbor, can I go to the hospital without getting in trouble?
answer: Yes — emergency rooms in California must treat you regardless of immigration status, and hospitals do not ask about or report immigration status. Emergency Medi-Cal covers ER care for people who would otherwise qualify, regardless of status. Please get treatment; burns can get serious fast. Community clinics and 211 can also help connect you to low-cost follow-up care.
topic: Medical needs, prescriptions, and hospital access

question: my house burned down do i still have to pay my electric bill
answer: No — contact your utility right away to stop billing on the destroyed property and ask about their disaster relief program. They can suspend charges, waive fees, and help transfer service if you're staying somewhere temporary. PG&E: 1-800-743-5000, SCE: 1-800-655-4555, SDG&E: 1-800-411-7343. If you have trouble getting a fair resolution, file a complaint with the CPUC at cpuc.ca.gov/consumer-support.

question: are schools closed tomorrow
answer: School closure decisions are made by your local school district, not by FEMA or the state. Check your district's website, social media, or local news for the most current information. You can also call 211 (or visit 211.org) for updates on closures in your area.

question: How long does FEMA take to decide on an appeal?
answer: FEMA typically decides appeals within 30 days of receiving them, but it can take up to 90 days. If they need more information, they'll contact you. You'll get the decision in writing — either by mail or in your DisasterAssistance.gov account.

question: my husband is a farmer and lost everything in the flood he wont eat or get out of bed im scared
answer: Please take this seriously — withdrawal and not eating after a major loss can signal severe depression. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) now to talk with someone who can help you figure out next steps; press 1 for the Veterans line if that applies. The Farm Aid hotline (1-800-FARM-AID) also offers crisis support specifically for farm families. If he talks about hurting himself or you can't wake him, call 911.
topic: Mental health and emotional support after a disaster

question: whats the differnce between fema and sba loan
answer: FEMA provides grants (money you don't pay back) for urgent needs like temporary housing, basic repairs, and essential items — but amounts are limited. SBA offers low-interest disaster loans (up to $500,000 for homes, $100,000 for personal property, more for businesses) to cover the rest. FEMA usually refers you to SBA automatically; you should complete the SBA application even if you don't want a loan, because it can unlock more FEMA grant money.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: Is there a way to get a backup battery or generator through my utility?
answer: PG&E's Portable Battery Program offers free or discounted portable batteries to Medical Baseline customers in high fire-threat areas. SCE and SDG&E have similar Critical Care Backup Battery programs. Contact your utility to check eligibility, and also ask about the Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP), which offers rebates for home battery systems through the CPUC.

question: Hi, we evacuated during the wildfires and now back home but my kids (8 and 11) are having nightmares and don't want to sleep alone, is this normal and what can I do to help them?
answer: Yes, nightmares and clinginess are very normal reactions for children after a disaster — it usually improves with time and support. Try keeping bedtime routines consistent, letting them sleep closer to you temporarily, talking openly about what happened in age-appropriate ways, and limiting exposure to disaster news. FEMA's Crisis Counseling Program offers free confidential support — call the Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 or text TalkWithUs to 66746. If nightmares persist beyond a month or worsen, reach out to their pediatrician or a child therapist.
topic: Emotional support for children after a disaster

question: my neighbor is burning debris in his yard is that allowed
answer: Open burning of fire debris is generally prohibited because the ash contains toxic materials like asbestos, lead, and heavy metals. Report it to your local Air Quality Management District and the county environmental health department. You can also call CAL FIRE if there's a fire safety concern.

question: I'm a small business owner in Altadena, my shop was destroyed. Does the tax extension cover my quarterly estimated taxes and payroll taxes too?
answer: Yes. The California wildfire relief covers individual and business returns, quarterly estimated tax payments, payroll and excise tax returns, and tax-exempt organization filings due during the relief period — all postponed to October 15, 2025. Payroll deposits due in the first days after the disaster also got penalty abatement. Call the IRS at 1-866-562-5227 to make sure your business is flagged for relief.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: can i get fema if im undocumented
answer: FEMA cash assistance generally requires at least one household member to be a U.S. citizen, non-citizen national, or qualified non-citizen — but a child with a Social Security number can apply on behalf of the whole family. Even without FEMA, you may qualify for help from the Red Cross, 211, local nonprofits, and the CA Disaster Relief Assistance for Immigrants (when activated). Call 211 to find immigrant-friendly recovery services in your county.

question: do i get my security depsoit back if the buildng was destroyd
answer: Yes — if your rental was destroyed or made uninhabitable by a disaster, your landlord must return your security deposit, minus any lawful deductions unrelated to the disaster damage. They generally have 21 days from when you vacate. Send a written request with your forwarding address. If they refuse, you can file in small claims court or get free help through Disaster Legal Services by calling 211.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: how do i file insurance claim after fire
answer: Call your insurance company's claims hotline as soon as possible to start your claim. Take photos and video of all damage before cleaning up, and make a list of damaged or destroyed items with approximate values. Keep receipts for any temporary lodging or emergency repairs — most policies reimburse these under Additional Living Expenses (ALE). If you need help, contact the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: how long do i have to aply for disater unemploment
answer: You generally have 30 days from the date DUA is announced for your disaster area to file your claim. Don't wait — apply as soon as possible through myEDD or by calling EDD at 1-800-300-5616. If you miss the deadline due to a good reason related to the disaster, explain that when you apply.

question: What documents do I need to apply for FEMA?
answer: Have ready: your Social Security number, current phone and mailing address, address of the damaged home, a brief description of damage, insurance information (policy number/company), household income, and a bank account/routing number for direct deposit. You don't need every document to start — apply right away at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362 and submit additional documents later.
topic: How to apply for disaster aid (eligibility, deadlines)

question: can my kid enroll in a diffrent school while ours is closed
answer: Yes. Under California's McKinney-Vento Act and AB 490, students displaced by disaster qualify as homeless/displaced and can immediately enroll in any school in the area they're staying — even without usual paperwork like proof of residency or records. Contact the new district's homeless liaison or registrar to enroll right away.

question: who cleans up burned house debris
answer: In California, CalRecycle runs the state debris removal program for state and federally-declared disasters. They work with Cal OES and local governments to remove contaminated debris from your property at no out-of-pocket cost. You'll need to sign a Right-of-Entry form with your county to opt in — check with your local recovery office for deadlines.

question: I run a small family farm co-op in Sonoma and we lost crops and equipment in the disaster. Are we eligible for SBA help?
answer: Yes, small agricultural cooperatives are explicitly eligible for SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL), and you can also apply for a Physical Disaster Loan to cover damaged equipment and structures — the two combined can total up to $2 million. Note that individual farms (not co-ops) typically go through USDA Farm Service Agency programs instead. Call SBA at 800-659-2955 to confirm your eligibility and start the application.

question: my elderly mom lives in pacific palisades and lost her home, she's never used a computer how does she get tax help
answer: She can call the IRS Disaster Assistance Hotline at 1-866-562-5227 to speak with a live agent who can flag her account for relief and answer questions. She can also visit a local IRS Taxpayer Assistance Center in person (call 1-844-545-5640 to schedule) or get free help from VITA volunteers at 211. Bring any tax records she has, even partial ones — the IRS can provide free transcripts of past returns.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: i have a bunch of canned food and baby suplies to donate where do they go
answer: Thanks for wanting to help! Please don't bring goods directly to shelters or burn zones — they often can't store or sort them. Call 211 or visit 211ca.org to find a local food bank or family resource center accepting those specific items. Baby supplies are often needed at Baby2Baby (baby2baby.org) and local diaper banks. Call ahead before dropping off so you know what they currently need.

question: can i bring my dog to the shelter
answer: Many California disaster shelters are pet-friendly or have a co-located animal shelter nearby, but not all. Call 211 before you go to confirm pet policies. Bring a leash, carrier, food, vaccination records, and any medications if possible. County animal services and the Humane Society often set up emergency pet shelters during major disasters.

question: hi so our whole neighborhood has been without internet and phone for like 5 days since the storm and my elderly mom needs to reach her doctor and i also need to file insurance stuff, is anyone doing anything about this or where can we go?
answer: I'm sorry you're dealing with this. A few things that can help: (1) Call 211 (or visit 211.org) to find nearby Disaster Recovery Centers, libraries, or community sites offering free Wi-Fi and phones. (2) Carriers like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile often waive fees and set up mobile cell sites (COWs) after disasters — check their outage maps and disaster response pages. (3) You can file a complaint or get help with your phone/internet provider through the CPUC at cpuc.ca.gov/consumer-support or 1-800-649-7570. For your mom's medical needs, if it's urgent call 911; otherwise many pharmacies and clinics have landlines you can use.

question: What documents do I need to apply for FEMA assistance?
answer: You'll need your Social Security number, current and pre-disaster address, a phone number, insurance information, total household annual income, a bank account for direct deposit, and a description of the damage. Having these ready will speed up your application at DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362.

question: I'm a farmworker in Ventura County and the fields I work at got destroyed. My boss said no more work. Can I get help?
answer: Yes, you may qualify for Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) if your county is in a federally declared disaster area. Farmworkers and seasonal workers are commonly covered. Apply through myEDD or call EDD at 1-800-300-5616 (Spanish available). Bring or be ready to provide proof of your recent earnings, like pay stubs or a letter from your employer.

question: do i still have to file taxes by april 15 if my house burned down
answer: No. If you live in a federally declared California wildfire disaster area, the IRS has automatically postponed your filing and payment deadlines — for the 2025 California wildfires, deadlines were extended to October 15, 2025. You don't need to apply; the IRS uses your address on file. Check irs.gov/disaster-relief for your specific deadline.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: My elderly mom uses a wheelchair and we need a shelter that can accommodate her, where do we go?
answer: Call 211 and tell them about her accessibility needs — they'll direct you to an ADA-accessible shelter or a functional-and-access-needs shelter, which has medical staff and accessible bathrooms/cots. If she has medical equipment, mention that too. You can also call your county Office of Emergency Services. For longer-term housing, FEMA offers Accessibility-related repair assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov.

question: what if i already applied for calfresh but havent heard anything
answer: Log in to BenefitsCal.com to check your case status, or call your county social services office directly. If it's been more than 30 days (or 3 days for expedited service) with no response, ask for a supervisor. You can also call 2-1-1 for help following up. Make sure they have your current phone number since they may have tried to reach you for an interview.
topic: Food and water assistance (CalFresh, food banks)

question: what documents do i need to send with my appeal
answer: It depends on why you're appealing. For more home repair money: send contractor estimates, repair receipts, and photos of damage. For housing assistance: send proof of occupancy (lease, utility bill) or ownership (deed, tax bill). For denied identity verification: send a government ID and Social Security documentation. Your FEMA letter lists the specific documents needed for your case — and remember to put your FEMA application and disaster numbers on every page.

question: what if i already filed an extension before the fires happened
answer: You're still covered. The disaster relief gives you additional time beyond your original extension — but note that the postponement applies to filing, not to payments that were already due before the disaster declaration. If you owe and missed the original payment, contact the IRS to discuss penalty abatement under the disaster provisions.
topic: Tax filing extensions and disaster tax relief

question: I'm 74 and live alone in Altadena, my house is gone and I don't really use computers, how do I get FEMA help?
answer: You can apply for FEMA assistance by phone — call 1-800-621-3362, available 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. local time, with multilingual support. You can also visit a Disaster Recovery Center in person where staff will help you apply and answer questions; call 211 to find the nearest one. If mobility is an issue, ask 211 about senior services and Red Cross caseworkers who can help in person.

question: I'm a 72-year-old widow and my house was damaged in the fire. I don't really understand loans and I'm scared of taking on debt at my age. Are there other options?
answer: That's a very reasonable concern. You're not required to accept an SBA loan even if approved — but it's worth applying, because being denied by SBA can unlock additional FEMA grant assistance (which doesn't have to be repaid). SBA loans also have low interest, no payments for 12 months, and you can decline the loan after approval. Call FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 or visit a Disaster Recovery Center for free in-person help walking through your options.
topic: SBA disaster loans for homeowners and businesses

question: Hi, I'm self-employed and I do landscaping work but all my clients' yards burned and nobody is hiring me right now. I heard regular unemployment doesn't cover self-employed people, is there anything I can apply for?
answer: Yes — Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) is specifically designed for self-employed workers and others who don't qualify for regular unemployment. If the President has declared a disaster in your area, you can apply through myEDD or by calling 1-800-300-5616. Have proof of your self-employment income (tax returns, 1099s, invoices) ready, since EDD will ask for it to calculate your benefit.

question: Does the IRS give farmers extra time to file taxes after a drought?
answer: Yes. The IRS regularly extends the deadline for farmers and ranchers to replace livestock sold due to drought (under IRC §1033(e)), giving you more time before having to recognize capital gains. In 2025, the IRS extended this relief to farmers and ranchers in 49 states (IR-2025-93). Your tax filing deadline may also be postponed if your county is in a federally declared disaster area — check irs.gov/disaster for the current list.

question: I'm a farmworker in Sonoma County and my truck is how I get to the fields every day, it got destroyed when the fire came through. I don't have papers but my truck was registered. Can I still get help?
answer: You may still qualify for help. FEMA requires at least one household member to have eligible immigration status (including a U.S. citizen child), but California also has state programs that don't require status — call 211 or visit a Local Assistance Center for referrals. Nonprofits like Catholic Charities and UndocuFund often provide direct cash assistance for vehicle replacement after disasters. Also check with your auto insurance regardless of status, since the policy itself is what matters for a claim.
topic: Replacing a car or vehicle damaged in disaster

question: i already applied but didnt mention im blind does that change anything
answer: Yes, it can — please update FEMA. Call the Helpline at 1-800-621-3362 and tell them you have a disability and need to add accommodations to your file. They can resend your decision letter in an accessible format (large print, Braille, audio, or email), assign a Disability Integration Advisor, and make sure any home inspection or follow-up communication works for you. If you were denied, you have 60 days from your letter to appeal, and lack of accessible communication can be grounds to revisit your case.
topic: Seniors and people with disabilities — special assistance

question: house burned down what do i do first
answer: First, make sure you and your family are safe and have shelter — call 211 for emergency shelter, food, and local disaster services. Then register with FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 or DisasterAssistance.gov, and contact your insurance company to start a claim. Do NOT re-enter your property until local officials say it's safe, and don't touch the ash — it's toxic.

question: I'm a senior living alone in Sonoma County and PG&E shut off my power for a PSPS, do I get any help?
answer: Yes — if you're on PG&E's Medical Baseline Program or self-identify as having access/functional needs, you may qualify for the Disability Disaster Access & Resources (DDAR) program, which can provide backup batteries, hotel stays, food replacement, or transportation during PSPS events. Call PG&E at 1-800-743-5000 to enroll in Medical Baseline, and contact your local Independent Living Center or 211 for DDAR help. Sonoma County also opens Community Resource Centers during PSPS with power, water, and Wi-Fi.

question: My landlord won't let me back in to get my belongings after the fire, what can I do?
answer: Tenants have a legal right to access their belongings even after a disaster, as long as the building is safe to enter. Send your landlord a written request (text or email is fine) for a specific time to retrieve items. If they continue to refuse, that may be an illegal lockout under Civil Code 789.3 — you can call local law enforcement for a civil standby, or contact Disaster Legal Services through 211 for free legal help.
topic: Renter rights and protections after disaster damage

question: my house didnt burn but theres smoke damage everywhere is that covered
answer: Yes — smoke, soot, and ash damage are typically covered under standard homeowners policies, even if the structure didn't burn. File a claim right away and document everything with photos. Don't try to clean it yourself; professional smoke remediation is usually covered and improper cleaning can make things worse. Also keep any items you've had to replace (food, HVAC filters, etc.) on your claim list.
topic: Filing insurance claims after a disaster

question: I'm 72 and I'm not great with computers — can someone help me file my appeal in person?
answer: Yes, you can take your appeal documents in person to a Disaster Recovery Center (DRC), where staff can help you submit them. To find the nearest DRC, call the FEMA Helpline at 1-800-621-3362 or visit DisasterAssistance.gov and use the DRC Locator. Bring your FEMA letter, your application number, and any documents supporting your appeal (repair estimates, receipts, etc.).

question: hi we've been without power for almost 3 days now after the storm and my husband uses an oxygen machine, is there anything we can do?
answer: Please call 911 or go to the nearest ER if his oxygen is running low — this is a medical emergency. Then contact your utility and ask to be added to their Medical Baseline Program, which flags your address for priority restoration and extra outage notifications (PG&E: 1-800-743-5000; SCE: 1-800-655-4555; SDG&E: 1-800-411-7343). Many counties also open cooling/charging centers during long outages — call 211 to find the closest one.

question: my parents are scared to go to the shelter because of ICE, is it safe?
answer: Disaster shelters in California do not ask about immigration status, and ICE has a long-standing policy of not conducting enforcement at shelters or disaster relief sites. Red Cross and county shelters serve everyone regardless of status, and California's SB 54 limits local cooperation with immigration enforcement. If they feel safer, they can also seek shelter through trusted community organizations — call 211 for a list in your area.
